To recruit, retain and support staff while preserving safe, high‑quality care, NHS workforce planning must prioritise clear scope‑of‑practice, robust revalidation and predictable indemnity arrangements. By setting explicit roles and boundaries, we give staff confidence to work at the top of their competence and make patient safety non‑negotiable. Complement this with funded protected clinical supervision and structured mentoring to support new roles such as advanced practitioners, pharmacist prescribers and care coordinators. 

Invest in interoperable, secure IT and ongoing staff digital training, enabling a common, accessible patient record across primary, community and urgent care. This should include reliable digital tools for triage and remote monitoring, while also safeguarding alternatives for digitally excluded patients—maintaining telephone triage, paper processes and local access points. 

The plan must align with flexible working, wellbeing and realistic workloads: targeted recruitment, faster onboarding, induction for international hires, protected admin time, and clear progression pathways. Multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, therapists and social care coordinators—must be empowered to handle routine issues so GPs can focus on complex care, with supervised support funded to ensure patient safety is maintained. This combination supports safer care, better job satisfaction, and sustainable workforce growth.

From where I sit in England, and after seeing how staff shortages ripple through GP practices, community teams and mental health services, any NHS workforce plan must be built with people at its core. It should clearly fund and protect career development, while also expanding the number of people entering and staying in primary care. At the same time, it must recognise the reality of digital transformation and protect alternatives for those who can’t or don’t wish to engage online. A well-designed plan would work in practice, not just on paper, and it would be measurable from day one.

- Funded career pathways, protected CPD, mentorship and return-to-practice schemes: One of the strongest levers to retain experienced clinicians and support early-career staff is to guarantee time and financial support for continuing education. Protected CPD time and funded mentorship can help younger clinicians grow confidence while experienced staff can refresh knowledge and gradually hand on expertise. Return-to-practice schemes are particularly valuable for those who stepped back for family or other reasons; with appropriate retraining and supervised placements, they can rejoin safely and contribute meaningfully. In my area I’ve seen colleagues take part in small, structured return-to-practice programs that made a real difference to morale and workload balance.

- Increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and university-practice partnerships: The supply pipeline must be widened, especially for primary care. Expanding nursing, allied health, pharmacists and GP training places, with guaranteed protected placements in real practice settings and strong university-practice partnerships, would help steady the flow of staff into the system. This would also support a more distributed workforce across urban and rural areas, where shortages bite hardest. My own practice area benefited when students could rotate through, and the presence of motivated junior staff often lifted team morale and patient care quality.

- Invest in interoperable IT, secure systems and staff digital training while safeguarding alternatives for digitally excluded patients: Digital tools should reduce administrative burden and help teams work smarter, not push people toward systems that exclude others. Interoperable, secure IT that connects NHS111, primary care and community services can improve safety and efficiency, provided staff have solid training and ongoing support. Yet we must not swap human contact for screens. For digitally excluded patients, there should always be clear non-digital routes to access care—phone lines with clinicians, outreach options, and in-person signposting. In practice, wherever IT upgrades have been rolled out, I’ve observed a drop in duplicated data entry and smoother patient handoffs, but I’ve also seen how poorly implemented tech can widen inequities if outreach and training are lacking.

- Safe staffing, skill mix and wellbeing: A workforce plan must set evidence-based targets for clinician-to-patient ratios, with a realistic mix of GPs, nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists and mental health professionals in each area. It should fund wellbeing supports, reduced administrative load, and reasonable workloads to prevent burnout. Inexperienced teams need mentoring and adequate supervision so patient safety isn’t compromised while they’re learning.

- Local delivery with transparent evaluation: Rollout should be piloted in a few areas with open data on wait times, staff retention, patient outcomes and satisfaction. This allows learning from what works and what doesn’t, and ensures resources aren’t poured into schemes that don’t deliver. I’d want to see pilots that genuinely test mentorship models, protected CPD time and university-led placements in real practice settings before wider adoption.

- Practical steps to align with broader service aims: Strengthen multidisciplinary teams at the primary care level, expanding roles for pharmacists, social prescribers and district nurses who can alleviate pressure on GPs and free up time for patients with complex needs. Encourage flexible working patterns and career ladders that keep experienced clinicians in front-line roles while still providing opportunities for career progression.

Overall, the plan should acknowledge that recruiting and retaining staff and maintaining high-quality care go hand in hand with sensible investment in training, clear career pathways, strong digital foundations, and equitable access for all patients. If executed with realism, transparency, and a focus on patient safety, these priorities could help reduce wait times and improve continuity of care for my neighbours and me, while protecting those who aren’t comfortable with digital solutions.

From my long experience of using NHS services in England, I think a workforce plan should prioritise three things that will actually make care safer and kinder. First, invest in interoperable IT and secure systems, coupled with real staff training in digital tools. Keep alternatives for digitally excluded patients—phone lines, easy-to-use booking, and paper forms—so nobody is left behind. I’ve seen how a simple, well‑run online system can save time, but also how hard it is for older residents who struggle with tech if there isn’t a safe fallback.

Second, deliver targeted incentives to hard-to-fill areas—rural, urban deprived and coastal communities—together with housing and transport support. Flexible working patterns and local recruiters can help keep GPs, nurses and therapists in place where they are most needed, avoiding long, exhausting commutes.

Third, cut unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks. Streamline referrals and boost IT usability so clinicians spend more time with patients and less time on admin. If we can free time for patient‑facing care and maintain parity with physical health services, care will be safer, more compassionate and more personal for older residents who value face-to-face contact.

Overall, a focused, humane plan that recognises digital inclusion and local supply gaps will sustain high‑quality care for everyone.

i strongly believe from my point of view, after years of watching services stretch to meet demand, I believe any NHS workforce plan should be built on sustainability and safety first, with a clear eye on real-world impact in local areas. I don’t want to see policy becoming another set of promises that doesn’t translate into calmer wards or more reliable appointments. Instead, I’d prioritise a mix of practical workforce foundations, flexible working, and smarter use of skills that actually supports patients and staff alike.

- Safe, sustainable staffing levels and retention. Plans must set and monitor safe staffing baselines for GP practices, district nursing, mental health teams, and community services. Relying on locums or overworking already stretched teams simply shifts the problem. Build stability with longer-term contracts where possible, predictable hours, and a proper pipeline that reduces last-minute gaps.
- Fair pay, progression and return-to-practice routes. Staff retention hinges on fair remuneration, clear career pathways, and welcoming routes for those returning after a break. Fund accessible training and mentorship so experienced nurses, therapists, and GPs feel valued and can stay in patient-facing roles rather than drifting away.
- Reduce administrative burden and simplify workflows. Clinicians spend too much time on paperwork and repetitive tasks. Invest in dedicated admin and digital tools that actually save time in clinical contact, not just add screens. This should free clinicians up to focus on direct patient care and reduce burnout.
- Strengthen multi-disciplinary teams and local leadership. A robust, well-supported MDT approach with clear roles helps patients navigate care without bouncing between services. Local leadership should have the resources to coordinate services, share workload, and ensure consistent access across primary, community and mental health care.
- Flexible, humane working patterns. Flexible hours, part-time leadership roles, and well-planned shift patterns help staff balance work with caring responsibilities and personal wellbeing. Rest breaks and safe rostering must be non-negotiable to prevent exhaustion and mistakes.
- Wellbeing, mental health and peer support for staff. Normalising mental health support, confidential counselling, and peer networks is essential. A workforce plan that neglects staff wellbeing is not sustainable and risks higher turnover or poorer care.
- Training pipelines and local recruitment. Strengthen local training partnerships with universities and apprenticeship routes to widen access and grow care teams from within communities. Target rural and underserved areas with incentives and tailored programs to reduce disparities in access to care.
- Expanded roles for non-doctor clinicians. Empower pharmacists, nurse practitioners, physiotherapists and allied health professionals to manage routine conditions and minor ailments where appropriate. This can free up GPs for more complex cases while improving access for patients who need quick care.
- Data-driven planning and transparency. Local health systems should publish clear workforce data—vacancies, turnover, caseloads, patient wait times—so communities can see how plans are delivering improvements. This also helps identify where pilots are working and where they’re not.
- Realistic, locally tailored pilots with robust evaluation. I’d want to see pilots tested in different settings, with explicit targets and public reporting on outcomes like wait times, safety indicators, and patient experience. If improvements aren’t material, adjust or halt quickly rather than sweeping changes across the board.

In short, any NHS workforce plan should aim for stable, well-supported teams working with adequate time and resources to deliver safe, high-quality care. It should respect frontline staff voices, protect against burnout, and keep patients at the centre with transparent progress signals. My experience suggests both the urgency of action and the need for careful, evidence-led implementation.
Prioritise integrated recruitment and joint funding across NHS, social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workloads and support holistic, safe care.

I believe any NHS workforce plan must prioritise getting the right people to the right places with the right support. Targeted, competitive pay and retention payments, plus relocation packages and bursaries, are essential to recruit in underserved areas and high‑demand roles such as GPs, district nurses and mental health staff. I’ve seen pilots where relocation support and bursaries helped attract clinicians to short-staffed communities, which is exactly what we need if we want sustainable local care.

Equally important is keeping people in the job long term. Flexible hours, part‑time and job‑share options, phased retirement, affordable childcare and proactive mental health and wellbeing services should be normal features of the offer. Safe, high‑quality care depends on staffing levels that match patient need, so the plan should fund robust training pipelines, clear career progression, protected time for supervision and peer support, and well‑defined workload standards.

This must align with the co‑located, multidisciplinary hubs I’ve advocated for: recruitment and retention policies backed by sustainable funding, transparent governance, and digital tools that support flexible, integrated working. When schemes are cohesive and adequately funded, you’ll get teams that grow together rather than in silos, delivering better care for communities.

absolutely i believe the NHS workforce plan should prioritise three things: growing the supply of primary care staff through education and training, strengthening retention to combat burnout, and attracting talent to underserved areas with targeted incentives. Specifically, we should increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships so new local clinicians can train and stay within the system. In my area, students report inconsistent placement opportunities; safeguarding these experiences would help build the domestic pipeline.

Retention matters just as much as recruitment. Flexible hours, part‑time or job‑share roles, phased retirement, accessible childcare, and proactive mental health support can keep skilled staff working where they are needed most and reduce burnout. For many colleagues, those measures would make the difference between staying and leaving.

To fill high‑demand roles and locations, targeted pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries are essential. Any expansion must accompany safe staffing levels, robust supervision, continuing professional development and modern IT, with clear governance. Earlier I mentioned the importance of integrated IT and governance to avoid fragmentation; this plan should ensure that!

I welcome a NHS workforce plan that strengthens recruitment and retention but keeps safety and quality at its core. Priorities must include clear safe-staffing ratios for GP practices, district nursing, and mental health teams, with independent reporting so patients know standards are being met. Continuity models matter: longer-term patient lists with the same GP and embedded, stable multidisciplinary teams in community clinics reduce repeated questions and mistakes and help older patients stay independent at home. Safety monitoring should be ongoing—regular audits of wait times, appointment durations, adverse events, and patient feedback loops to learn and act quickly.

In practice this means cap workloads, protect time for training and handovers, and ensure cover during holidays without piling onto a few clinicians. I’ve seen how, when a nurse or GP is unexpectedly absent, care slows and risks rise; with reserve staff and cross-trained teams, access can stay timely without compromising safety. Remote triage can help, but it must escalate appropriately to a clinician when safety signals appear. Targeted recruitment should go hand in hand with robust induction and wellbeing support to keep people safe and motivated in the long term.

I think an NHS workforce plan should prioritise funded career pathways across all roles, with protected CPD time and structured mentorship and return-to-practice schemes. These elements help retain experienced clinicians and support early-career staff, making it less likely people leave for better development opportunities elsewhere. In practice, that means funded training programmes, dedicated CPD budgets, formal supervision for new recruits, and fast-track return-to-work routes for those who paused careers. On recruitment, we need targeted competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries to attract staff to underserved areas and to high-demand roles such as mental health, geriatrics and general practice in hard-to-staff settings. These incentives should be tailored to place-specific needs—rural, urban deprived and coastal areas—with housing and transport support to recruit and retain people who might otherwise go elsewhere. Crucially, these measures must accompany safe-care safeguards: appropriate staffing ratios, manageable rosters, and robust mentoring and governance so patient safety isn’t compromised. From my experience navigating care for family members, stability and visible development opportunities are what keep staff in roles and build public trust.

A strong NHS workforce plan should be built around safe, high‑quality care while expanding the numbers and skills of the workforce in a way that is locally sustainable. In practice, that means a clear framework for what staff can do (scope‑of‑practice), robust revalidation processes, and reliable indemnity arrangements, all supported by funded, protected clinical supervision as new roles are introduced. It also means targeted financial incentives to attract people to harder‑to‑staff areas and high‑demand roles. 

- Clarify scope‑of‑practice, governance and revalidation: Establish explicit, locally adaptable scopes of practice for each role (GPs, nurses, allied health professionals, physician associates, mental health workers, social prescribers, etc.) with agreed protocols for delegation and escalation. Tie these to clear governance and patient‑safety requirements so teams know who can do what, when, and how they are supervised. Ensure revalidation is protected by dedicated time and administrative support, so staff maintain their qualifications without being pulled away from patient care. 

- Fund indemnity and protection for new roles: Ensure all staff taking on expanded or different responsibilities have appropriate indemnity arrangements that are affordable and straightforward to access. This reduces anxiety about practice risk and helps retain staff who might otherwise seek roles with clearer cover. 

- Fund protected clinical supervision: Invest in protected supervision time for newly trained staff and those taking on expanded responsibilities. This should include structured mentoring, regular case discussions, and clinical supervision that is practically integrated into the working week, not as an add‑on. The aim is to build confidence, maintain patient safety, and support retention as people develop new skills. Personally, when a few colleagues moved into broader mental health and district nurse roles, the difference was tangible once supervision was consistently available and respected in the timetable.

- Targeted pay, retention and relocation support: To recruit and retain in underserved and high‑demand areas, combine competitive pay with retention bonuses, relocation packages and bursaries for training, especially in nursing, allied health, GP training and mental health posts. Clear conditions on how bursaries or incentives are earned—and what happens if someone leaves early—are essential to avoid short‑term gains with long‑term gaps. In my community, targeted incentives helped bring in a couple of district nurses who stayed because their costs were supported and they could see a viable career path locally.

- Career pathways and continuing development: Expand apprenticeships and alternative routes into registered roles with transparent competency milestones, academic credit and guaranteed progression. Link CPD to service planning and local workforce needs so staff can see a tangible route forward rather than feeling stuck. Funding for CPD should be protected and aligned with the needs of local teams and patients who currently struggle to access timely care.

- Equity across geographies: Prioritise expansion in rural and coastal areas where access is worse. Use realistic staffing targets, long‑term funding commitments and partnerships with local training providers to establish sustainable pipelines. Balance is key: we need to grow the workforce without creating churn elsewhere or overburdening those already in post.

- Implementation and safety metrics: Build the plan around patient safety indicators, staff wellbeing and rotas that prevent burnout. Data should guide where more supervision, training or recruitment is needed. Regular audits of scope adherence, incident reporting and patient experience will help keep high quality as numbers grow.

In practice, a cohesive plan that normalises expanded roles only with strong safety nets—clear scopes, robust revalidation, dependable indemnity, funded supervision, and meaningful financial incentives—will persuade staff to move into underserved areas and stay long enough to make a real difference. My priority is for a plan that treats workforce growth as an investment in safe, sustainable patient care, not a quick fix that leaves gaps in a few years. A well‑funded, well‑managed rollout—with local leadership and accountability—can help deliver timely access and high‑quality care for people who currently struggle most to get it.

I think any NHS workforce plan should be built from what actually keeps services safe, high-quality and accessible in practice: good data, sustainable staffing, and flexible, people-centered support for those delivering care. It needs to be locally focussed so teams on the ground can see what works for their patients and staff, and it should be measurable so funding and improvements can be tracked over time.

Key priorities I’d like to see are:

- Local, transparent data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks. Trusts and primary care networks should publish clear, locally relevant dashboards showing staffing levels by role and shift, patient demand and wait times, vacancy and turnover rates, sickness absence, and patient safety indicators. That data should feed live planning: when a ward or practice is stretched, modelling can forecast the impact of adding a clinician, changing shift patterns, or creating a new role (for example nurse-led triage). Evaluation frameworks must link actions to outcomes so we can learn what actually reduces waiting times without compromising care quality.

- Safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models. We need to guard against my experience of stretched teams where quality slips. Commit to safe staffing ratios in critical areas (A&E, urgent care, district nursing, mental health crisis teams) and embed continuity of care where possible so patients consistently see familiar clinicians. Teams with stable rosters and predictable supervision tend to deliver safer care and better patient experience. Real-time safety monitoring and integrated incident reporting should be part of workforce planning, not after the event.

- Flexible hours and diverse retention strategies. To recruit and keep a broad, capable workforce, and to support existing staff who juggle caring responsibilities or long commutes, we should offer flexible hours, part-time options, job-sharing, and phased retirement. Practical measures include weekend/evening clinics only where feasible, but also robust backfill arrangements so staff aren’t left overloaded when they take on flexible shifts. Childcare support, proactive mental health services for staff, and structured return-to-work pathways after leave or burnout are essential. In my experience, colleagues are much more willing to stay in longer professional roles if their work-life balance is respected and their mental health needs are taken seriously.

- Career development, training and admin relief. A sustainable workforce plan should fund ongoing training, leadership development, and clear progression routes—from enhanced nursing roles to allied health professionals—so staff can grow without feeling they must leave for advancement. Reducing unnecessary admin load and providing dedicated clerical support frees clinicians to focus on patients, which in turn supports safer care.

- Integrated recruitment and retention across services. Local recruitment campaigns aligned with the needs of GP practices, community services and mental health teams help build a coherent, fully staffed system. This includes practical support for newcomers (orientation, peer buddies, local induction) and, where appropriate, responsible use of targeted international recruitment to fill shortages with appropriate safeguarding and integration measures.

- Governance, funding alignment and accountability. Funding should be tied to clear workforce plans with milestones and public reporting. Local teams must have decision-making power to adapt staffing to changing patient flows, with oversight that ensures changes don’t undermine access or safety. Frontline staff should have a voice in designing rosters and workflows, because they know where bottlenecks occur and what supports actually reduce burnout.

From my perspective, implementing these elements would help sustain access improvements I’ve advocated for—so people can get timely GP or community care without compromising safety. When teams are well-supported, more predictable in their hours, and backed by transparent data and local tailoring, the system becomes more resilient. That continuity and August calm of staffing enables a more reliable schedule for patients and a fairer, safer environment for clinicians.

In short, a workforce plan that prioritises local data, safe staffing, flexible working, and strong development and wellbeing support is the right foundation for maintaining high-quality care while expanding access. I’d support swift pilots that test these ideas in different localities and publish the results so we can scale what works and adjust what doesn’t.

Prioritise sustainable recruitment, including streamlined visas and credential recognition for overseas staff, with robust integration support and retention, while safeguarding source health systems and maintaining rigorous training and safe staffing.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise safe, sustainable staffing across primary care, community services and mental health, with realistic headroom to cope with winter pressures. Key priorities: 1) recruiting from local communities and returning-to-practice schemes to build a stable, culturally competent workforce; 2) offering flexible, family-friendly working patterns, part-time routes, predictable hours and reduced administrative burden to improve retention; 3) supporting staff with protected time for training, supervision and multidisciplinary case discussions to maintain high care standards; 4) strong wellbeing and mental-health support for staff, including confidential counselling and debriefing after difficult cases; 5) safer staffing models and governance to reduce reliance on agency staff and ensure the right skill mix; 6) clear career progression and leadership pathways to retain experienced clinicians in the system; 7) investment in digital tools and robust IT that actually saves time rather than adds admin; 8) closer collaboration with social care and community groups to share workload and reduce avoidable hospital visits. In practice, when services feel stretched, patients and carers notice gaps in continuity and safety. Local neighbourhood teams, familiar with our area, are essential for sustaining trust and quality while easing workloads across the system.

From my perspective, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams and ensuring responsible overseas recruitment, alongside robust training and strong supervision, to safely redistribute GP workload while preserving high-quality care.

Prioritise multidisciplinary teams that can take on routine and growing tasks from GPs. This means expanding roles for nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied health professionals, with clear scopes of practice, standardised training, and robust supervision. In practice, this would involve
- formal recognition and credentialing for expanded scopes of practice, including independent or remotely supported prescribing where appropriate.
- explicit governance structures so every task shifted from a GP has a named supervisor and defined escalation path to avoid safety gaps.
- integrated care models where pharmacists lead medication reviews, PAs perform minor procedures and care coordination, and nurses run triage and chronic disease management with access to real-time decision support in shared digital records.
- protected supervision time and predictable workload planning, so the additional team members don’t become a further source of stress for clinicians.

Pair expansion with training and development. A sustainable plan must grow the pipeline: more local training places, return-to-practice schemes, apprenticeships for allied health professionals, and ongoing CPD. This helps retain staff who trained locally and makes it easier to fill vacancies without rushing staff into burnout. Pairing new roles with structured career ladders and management pathways keeps people motivated and reduces turnover.

Use data-driven workforce planning and safe task-shifting. Real-time dashboards should track staffing levels, patient demand, wait times, and safety indicators. This supports dynamic rostering, avoids overloading teams, and helps identify where additional MDT capacity is most needed (e.g., long-term care, mental health liaison, or chronic disease clinics).

Responsible overseas recruitment. Bringing in staff from abroad can be part of the solution, but it must be done responsibly. Streamlined visa processes and credible credential recognition are essential, but they should be coupled with strong integration support: orientation, language training if required, mentorship, and local induction to align with NHS practices and patient safety standards.
- Safeguards to health systems in source countries are crucial. I’d expect clear bilateral or multilateral arrangements that avoid hollowing out partner countries’ own health services, potentially including capacity-building commitments, rotations that allow returns, and limits on staffing exports tied to home-country needs.
- Practical integration supports include bridging programs, supervised placements, and mentoring to help overseas colleagues work safely and confidently within UK systems, while maintaining high standards of care.

Safeguards and culture. A safe, high-quality service requires manageable workloads and a culture of support, not just numbers. Practices should have protected time for supervision and professional development, reasonable caseload caps for new roles, and regular clinical governance reviews to ensure patient safety remains front and centre as the workforce evolves.

In short, a successful NHS workforce plan should grow and regulate multidisciplinary teams, expand and streamline safe overseas recruitment with strong integration safeguards, and tie everything to transparent training, governance and data-driven staffing. With those elements in place, we can relieve GP workload without compromising safety or care quality, and build a resilient workforce able to meet future demand.

Thank you for the opportunity to contribute. From our experience in areas where GP and community services are already stretched, any NHS workforce plan must prioritise both attracting the right people to the right places and supporting them so they can deliver safe, high‑quality care every day. The priorities below reflect what would make a real difference on the ground and align with our wider goals of more local, accessible, person‑centred services.

- Targeted competitive pay and relocation support to underserved areas and high‑demand roles: We need clear incentives to recruit and retain staff where there are shortages, including retention payments for frontline roles, relocation packages to help staff move to rural or hard‑to‑staff areas, and bursaries or sponsored training for students and newly qualified clinicians who commit to service in underserved communities. In our area, dedicated payments tied to longer‑term commitments help teams stabilise when vacancies repeatedly churn staff away.

- Flexible, safe and sustainable working conditions: Staff wellbeing is not optional. A workforce plan should mandate safe staffing levels, sensible workloads, protected time for supervision and continuing professional development, and flexible or extended hours where appropriate to match local service needs. The goal is to enable teams to deliver consistent, high‑quality care without burnout, which ultimately protects patients and reduces avoidable safeguarding or safety incidents.

- Multidisciplinary, local teams with clear career paths: Develop multi‑disciplinary teams anchored by a navigator or link worker, who can guide patients through primary, community and mental health services. Clear progression routes, upskilling, and leadership opportunities for nurses, allied health professionals and social care staff will help retain experienced practitioners and attract newcomers who want to work in integrated, community‑based settings.

- Interoperable, secure IT systems with comprehensive staff training: Investment in interoperable electronic records, shared care plans, and secure data sharing is essential. Staff need user‑friendly IT and reliable connectivity to deliver timely care, whether in a clinic, on the doorstep, or in a telehealth hub. We must also recognise the learning curve: formal digital training, ongoing cyber‑security education, and super‑user support within teams are necessary to avoid workflow disruptions and data breaches.

- Digital access with safeguards for digitally excluded patients: As we move to more digital options, we must ensure alternatives remain for those who cannot or do not wish to use online tools. This means maintaining telephone triage, in‑person appointments, and walk‑in slots, with staff trained to identify who would benefit from non‑digital routes. Flexible IT solutions should support both clinicians and patients, without widening health inequalities.

- Targeted recruitment pipelines and local partnerships: Build partnerships with universities, veterinary and healthcare schools, and local employers to promote NHS careers in our communities. Expand apprenticeships and placement opportunities in primary care, mental health and social care settings to grow a resilient pipeline of staff who understand local needs.

- Wellbeing, safety and protection of staff: Implement visible wellbeing support, protected breaks, mental health resources, and fatigue management. Safe working environments—proper PPE, safe transport when visiting patients in rural locations, and risk assessment at home visits—are non‑negotiable foundations for high‑quality care.

- Data‑driven planning with governance and accountability: Use real‑time workforce data to anticipate shortages, match training to anticipated demand, and deploy staff where they will deliver the most value. Pilot sites (3–5) can test governance, data sharing, consent and performance metrics before scaling up, with transparent reporting to commissioners and the public.

In practice, a stronger NHS workforce plan would mean more stable teams, better morale, and, crucially, care that patients can rely on in the places they live. For example, where we’ve introduced targeted retention payments and local relocation support, vacancy rates in community nursing have started to fall, and sick leave has reduced in the first year of a programme. When teams are equipped with interoperable IT and supported by robust training, clinicians spend less time wrestling with systems and more time with patients, which also supports better safety and outcomes.

We’re ready to participate in pilots and work with commissioners to translate these priorities into tangible, locally tailored actions that keep our services resilient and our patients safer, closer to home.

From my perspective living in Scotland and drawing on what I’ve seen in our communities, any NHS workforce plan must place recruiting and retaining staff in hard‑to‑fill places at its heart, while guaranteeing safe, high‑quality care for patients of all ages. In particular, I’d like to see a clear focus on tailored incentives for rural, coastal, and urban deprived areas, plus practical support to get people to relocate, settle in, and stay long term.

- Targeted incentives for hard‑to‑fill areas: The plan should include flexible, place‑based packages that recognise the extra challenges of rural and coastal posts. This could mean enhanced pay or allowances for rural/remote posts, housing or relocation support, and practical measures such as shorter training pathways combined with strong mentorship. It’s not just about numbers; it’s about making a career in those communities financially viable and personally sustainable.

- Housing and transport support: Access to affordable housing near clinics and reliable transport options are essential. In hard‑to‑fill areas, even modest housing assistance or a travel subsidy can make the difference between someone applying for a post and staying for years. I’ve heard of younger colleagues who would have gone elsewhere without a housing option close to work, and older staff who worry about long commutes in bad weather. These supports help staff feel anchored and able to focus on patient care.

- Training, CPD and clear career paths: A sustainable workforce needs regular, funded CPD, mentoring, and opportunities for return‑to‑practice after breaks. I’d like to see more apprenticeships and return‑to‑practice pathways, with supportive supervision and protected time for learning. That not only lifts skill levels but also improves morale and retention, particularly for rural and coastal teams where turnover can be high.

- Safe staffing and manageable workloads: The plan must set and maintain safe staffing levels across disciplines—GPs, nurses, therapists—so teams aren’t stretched thin. Flexible staffing pools, smarter rostering, and pragmatic workload management would help preserve care quality and reduce burnout.

- Local recruitment pipelines and civic partnerships: Strengthening links with schools, colleges, and universities to create local routes into primary care and community services is important. I’ve seen community placements, once well supported, lead to lasting commitments. Local recruitment with clear pathways is more likely to bring people who want to stay and serve their communities.

- Wellbeing, leadership and supportive work environments: Good line management, mentoring, opportunities for career progression, and access to wellbeing services are essential. Staff are more likely to stay when they feel valued, listened to, and able to balance work with their personal responsibilities.

- Balanced use of digital and non‑digital care tools: Digital systems can help with efficiency, but they must not come at the expense of patient care or staff workload. I’d like to see investment in robust IT support, remote triage, and e‑consults, while preserving non‑digital routes (telephone triage, in‑person clinics, local hubs) for those who rely on them. In particular, staff in rural and coastal areas often face connectivity challenges, so reliable infrastructure matters as much as the tools themselves.

- Monitoring and accountability: The plan should include clear, public targets and regular reporting on vacancies, turnover, patient safety indicators, and access to services. This helps communities see the impact of investments and keeps the focus on safe, high‑quality care.

In short, a workforce plan that truly supports Scotland’s older residents, rural communities, and coastal towns will blend targeted, place‑based incentives with strong training, housing and transport support, safe staffing, leadership development, and flexible, well‑supported working arrangements. When funded and monitored with care, these elements can stabilise teams, improve continuity of care in every neighbourhood, and keep high‑quality services within reach for everyone.

Prioritise clear scope-of-practice, robust revalidation, and indemnity arrangements; fund protected clinical supervision for new roles; develop transparent, localised workforce data, KPIs and evaluation frameworks to guide planning, funding and performance while safeguarding patient safety.

From living in England and balancing work and family, a NHS workforce plan should recognise that recruiting more staff is not enough unless we fund and support them to stay, care for patients safely, and maintain quality. Priorities must include sustainable staffing levels with stable funding so practices can plan long term, expanded training posts in general practice and community services, and accessible return-to-practice routes for those who paused. We also need strong wellbeing and workload safeguards: manageable caseloads, protected supervision time, easy access to mental health support, and targeted efforts to reduce admin burden so clinicians can spend time with patients rather than chasing forms. In practice this means guaranteeing weekends/evenings where possible and investing in multidisciplinary teams that share triage and back-office tasks. Local flexibility matters: different areas have different needs, so cross-skilling and clear career pathways help retain staff. Leadership and recognition matter too; staff must feel supported and valued. The plan should include clear metrics on vacancies, sickness, training capacity, and patient safety indicators, with ongoing funding tied to improving those measures.

I think any NHS workforce plan should put transparent, localised data at its core. Without verifiable local information, detailed modelling and clear KPIs, planning, funding and performance monitoring will remain guesswork and risk repeating the inequities and misallocations we already see. In our area, recruitment and retention pressures are real: practices rely on locums and agency staff, but there’s little real-time visibility beyond annual dashboards. A proper plan must require clinicians, local authorities, CCGs and trusts to publish unified workforce data at a practice and locality level—vacancy and turnover rates, time-to-fill, rosters, training pipelines, staff wellbeing indicators, and patient-safety outcomes linked to staffing levels.

We also need explicit evaluation frameworks. How do changes affect continuity of care, appointment access, wait times, triage quality, and capacity for home visits? Modelling should be locally grounded and scenario-based, with funding and incentives tied to safe staffing and measurable patient outcomes, not just headcount. Governance must ensure data quality, public reporting and flexible funding that follows the evidence. If we don’t demand this transparency and local accountability, reforms risk fragmentation and waste, undermining both timely access and safety for patients.”

From where I stand in England, the NHS workforce plan must prioritise three interconnected areas to recruit, retain and support staff without compromising safety. First, responsible overseas recruitment: create streamlined visa routes and faster credential recognition, coupled with strong integration support—language help, cultural induction and mentoring—to help newcomers settle and work confidently. Importantly, there must be safeguards to avoid draining health systems in source countries, including ethical recruitment codes and targeted schemes aligned to genuine local shortages. Second, safe staffing and continuity: establish clear staffing ratios by role and setting, and promote continuity-preserving team structures so patients see familiar staff and handovers don’t erode safety. Real-time staffing dashboards and robust safety monitoring should alert managers to rising risk. Third, defined scope and supported development: clarify scope-of-practice for new roles, ensure smooth revalidation, and secure indemnity arrangements with funded, protected clinical supervision for those taking on expanded duties. This should be complemented by local training and development—return-to-practice routes, CPD, apprenticeships—to grow the workforce at home. In practice, when newcomers are properly integrated and supervised, access improves and care quality remains high rather than being compromised.

I think the NHS workforce plan must be built around three core priorities that reflect what I see locally and what wouldd support timrly, high-quality care. First, tailored incentives for hard-to-fill areas—rural, urban deprived, and coastal communities—paired with housing and transport support, relocation grants and flexible working. Without staff willing to move or stay in those places, access gaps persist, especially for after-hours and community services. Second, secure multi-year funding that is ring-fenced for workforce initiatives A longer horizon means training capacity, staff drvelopment, and reliable service deliver without sudden policy shifts derailing new roles or rotations. Third, expanding training capacity: more undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong uni-practice partnerships. This builds domestic supply for primary care and reduces reliance on temporary staffing. In my experience, local clinics struggle to fill posts; stable funding and targeted local incentives would allow more apprenticeships, nurse practitioners, and GP trainees to be supported locally. That would feed into more flexible, accessible care suc as after-hours clinics and telehealthh hubs.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise recruiting, retaining and supporting staff in ways that keep care safe and manageable, not just expanding numbers. Targeted competitive pay and retention payments, plus relocation packages and bursaries, are essential to attract nurses, GPs and therapists to underserved areas and high-demand roles. Funding should underpin real career progression, strong supervision and protected time for continuing professional development so staff feel supported rather than burned out. 

Crucially, the plan must strengthen links with social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workload and enable holistic patient care. Joint funding and integrated staffing solutions can reduce handoffs and delays for patients. Flexible, family-friendly working patterns, improved staffing ratios, and better workload planning are needed to guard safety. 

From my area, repeated staff shortages and wait-lists show how attrition hurts access; where there is joint investment, services feel more resilient. I’d also like to see administration lightened by practical support and digital tools that genuinely save time, plus ongoing supervision and well-being resources for staff. A long-term, stable funding commitment is vital to avoid cycling back to short-term fixes and to sustain safe, high-quality care.

From my point of view living in England, a strong NHS workforce plan should prioritise sustainable, long‑term investment and practical changes that keep patient care front and centre. I’ve seen how staffing pressures ripple through waiting times and the quality of care, so the plan needs to be realistic, measurable and mindful of frontline realities.

First, secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlements enabling sustained workforce initiatives, training capacity and reduced short-term policy volatility. This would mean predictable funding for GP training posts, nursing and allied health professional pipelines, and return‑to‑practice schemes, so clinicians aren’t caught in a cycle of short-lived commitments. It would also provide guaranteed resources for interpreters and language support, which links directly to my experience of language barriers turning into delays and misunderstandings for patients and their families.

Second, reduce unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks, streamline referrals and improve IT usability to free clinician time for patient‑facing care. Clinicians shouldn’t spend hours chasing forms or waiting on systems that don’t interoperate. A simpler referral workflow, better decision support in electronic records, and a single, longitudinal view of a patient across primary, community and mental health services would save time and reduce risk. When I’ve tried to navigate multiple portals, it’s clear how much time is diverted away from direct patient contact.

Third, strengthen recruitment and retention through flexible workforce models and supportive working conditions. That means safer rostering, protected time for continuous professional development, and clear pathways for career progression. Practical steps include expanding nurse prescriber roles, more pharmacist‑led clinics to alleviate routine workloads, and targeted international recruitment with comprehensive onboarding and supervision to maintain care quality while expanding capacity.

Fourth, strengthen links with social care, mental health and community services through joint funding and shared workforce planning to redistribute workload and improve holistic patient care. Multidisciplinary teams that can address medical needs alongside social determinants have the potential to prevent crises and reduce unnecessary hospital use. In practice, a jointly funded community hub with a common rota and single point of contact would cut down repeated handoffs and delays for families managing chronic conditions.

Fifth, prioritise staff wellbeing and safety as a core component of quality care. Burnout is a patient safety issue. Plans should ensure reasonable shift patterns, access to mental health support for staff, safe working environments, and channels to raise frontline concerns without fear of reprisals. Supporting the people who provide care is essential to sustaining high standards over the long term.

Finally, deliver robust governance with clear milestones, independent evaluation and ongoing feedback that includes input from frontline staff and patient groups. Co‑design with unions and professional bodies helps ensure the plan is ambitious but practical, adaptable and anchored in real-world delivery. If these elements are aligned, the NHS workforce plan can recruit, retain and support skilled clinicians and other staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care that patients experience in every area.

From our experience across rural England, the biggest challenge is sustaining staffing levels while keeping care safe and local. A practical NHS workforce plan should prioritise three things: expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams; securing long-term, ring-fenced funding; and offering genuinely flexible, supportive working arrangements to retain staff.

First, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams. Give nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied roles clear scopes of practice, robust training, and supervision within rural hubs so they can share routine GP workloads without compromising safety. Establish joint clinics and shared care pathways, with governance and regular audits to prove patient outcomes improve. Remote supervision should be available where travel to larger centres is difficult.

Second, lock in multi-year funding. A stable, ring-fenced settlement is essential for expanding training capacity, creating sustainable recruitment incentives, and protecting supervision time and backfill. Avoid the short-term policy churn that disrupts planning and undermines morale.

Third, provide genuine flexibility and support to retain staff. Flexible hours, job-sharing, phased retirement, affordable childcare, and proactive mental health services help reduce burnout and keep a diverse workforce in rural areas.

Finally, invest in local training capacity and rural training hubs, with funded placements and strong links to universities. Combine this with better IT and reduced admin burden so clinicians can devote time to patients. This combination is what’s needed to maintain safe, high-quality care in our communities.

A sustainable NHS workforce plan must prioritise safe staffing, equitable recruitment, and strong support to retain skilled staff, while guarding the quality of care for patients. In particular, I believe overseas recruitment can play a constructive role when it is responsible, well-regulated and embedded in a broader people strategy. The plan should therefore focus on the following priorities:

- Streamlined overseas recruitment and rapid credential recognition: create clear, time‑bound visa routes for frontline clinical staff, with priority processing for essential roles in general practice, nursing and allied health. Pair this with fast, robust credential verification and recognition processes so qualified professionals can begin contributing sooner. Ensure language and communication skills are assessed and supported early, not as a bottleneck after arrival.

- Comprehensive integration support: provide structured induction, mentorship, and a formal buddy system that helps overseas recruits navigate NHS culture, local guidelines, and interdisciplinary teamwork. Offer language and cultural competence training, access to welcoming communities and housing guidance, and flexible start dates to ease settling in.

- Safeguards for source countries and ethical recruitment: commit to international partnerships that avoid “draining” health systems. Invest in training capacity in source countries, establish return‑of‑service or mutual capacity‑building agreements, and set reasonable quotas tied to workforce needs and ethical recruitment principles. Regularly publish data on recruitment sources, to ensure transparency and public accountability.

- A strong domestic pipeline alongside international recruitment: expand domestic training places for nurses, GPs, pharmacists and allied health professionals; support return‑to‑practice pathways, career progression, and longer-term development. This should be complemented by clear, fair progression routes for overseas‑trained staff to higher responsibilities as they gain experience in the NHS.

- Retention and workforce wellbeing: reduce burnout by ensuring safe staffing ratios and realistic workloads, with dependable supervision and mentorship. Improve pay progression and recognition for experienced staff, and strengthen wellbeing and mental health support, including flexible working patterns, family-friendly policies, and access to affordable childcare when possible.

- Integration into teams and local communities: pairing new staff with local mentors, providing housing and community integration support, and promoting inclusive workplace cultures so teams feel cohesive quickly. Regular, constructive feedback loops with line managers should be standard to address concerns early and keep morale high.

- Safety, quality, and data‑driven planning: use real‑time dashboards to monitor staffing levels, patient outcomes, and wait times so recruitment and deployment decisions are evidence‑led. Ensure robust clinical governance and safeguarding safeguards remain central as new staff join teams.

- Clear ethical and governance standards: enforce fair employment practices, equal access to training, and protections against exploitation. Make sure recruitment practices adhere to professional standards and that patient safety is never compromised by speed of onboarding.

From my own experience in England, when overseas‑qualified staff join our practice with strong onboarding and clear supervision, patient care improves quickly—more consistent availability for appointments, better language support for diverse patients, and a calmer, more experienced team. But it can take longer to register and to integrate, which delays their impact. A plan that accelerates visa and credential checks, pairs new staff with mentors, and provides targeted integration support would translate into shorter waits for patients and more reliable care for people with complex needs.

Ultimately, the NHS benefits from a diverse and skilled workforce, provided recruitment is ethical, sustainable and paired with robust domestic development. If the workforce plan combines responsible overseas recruitment with strong retention, professional development, and a commitment to safe, high‑quality care, it will help rebuild resilience in our services while protecting both patients and workers.

i strongly believe to recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the plan should prioritise three pillars. Second, strengthen links with social care, mental health and community services. Fund joint roles and shared care pathways so workload is redistributed, delivering holistic care and reducing avoidable hospital attendances. Third, cut admin burden and streamline processes. In practice, this means better electronic referral flows and shared care plans, plus protected time for consultations. In Wales, a workforce plan for NHS services must be built on long-term stability. My sense from recent winters and busy periods is that short-term tinkering with staffing, pay bands or training slots creates more fragility than it fixes. If we want safe, high-quality care that patients can rely on, we need secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding that underwrites sustained workforce initiatives, expands training capacity and reduces policy volatility that disrupts recruitment and planning.

Priorities I’d like to see prioritised in an NHS workforce plan:

- Long-term, ring-fenced funding for recruitment and training. This should cover undergraduate and postgraduate training places, return-to-practice schemes, and dedicated funding to expand the capacity of GP, nursing, allied health professional, and mental health pipelines. In practice, this could mean new university–NHS partnerships in Wales to grow local hubs for skills development, more residency-type posts for pharmacists and physiotherapists, and extended training places that align with actual service needs rather than political cycles.

- Expand the training capacity and trainee support. We need more placements, more supervision capacity, and protected time for staff to teach and mentor. The aim should be to shorten the distance between qualification and confident, independent practice so new clinicians join the workforce ready to contribute from day one. If trainees see a clear path to progression and job security, retention will improve.

- Safe staffing and realistic workloads. A credible plan must commit to staffing levels that reflect patient demand, with robust mechanisms to monitor workload and fatigue. This means staffing tools that forecast peaks, reliable recruitment during aggressive winter periods, and funds to keep teams together rather than shuffling staff between sites. Wellbeing and mental health support for staff—counselling, peer support, and flexible working options—should be embedded in the core plan, not treated as an add-on.

- Clear career progression and leadership development. Frontline staff often stay when they feel valued and see a path forward. We should invest in leadership training for frontline managers and specialism-specific development tracks so people can specialise without leaving the patient-facing work they joined to do. Mentoring, structured appraisal processes, and recognition schemes could help reduce turnover.

- Broad, skill-mmix and role redesign with proper oversight. The plan should promote better use of skill mix across disciplines—for example enabling trained nurses, physiotherapists, and pharmacists to take on more autonomous, appropriate roles where safe and clinically sound. This would ease GP workload and improve patient flow, tying in with the reforms I’ve supported earlier around triage and navigation. It also means robust training for non-clinical roles in triage, care navigation, and digital support so that every team functions at its best.

- Fast, fair recruitment and retention pathways. Wales faces workforce shortages in key areas. A coherent plan should simplify recruitment channels, provide relocation and settlement support where needed, and ensure regulatory or credentialing barriers don’t unnecessarily slow a capable clinician from starting work. Consider targeted incentives for hard-to-fill areas and rural posts, paired with decent onboarding and supervision.

- Data-informed planning and accountability. There must be transparent, accessible data on vacancy rates, turnover, time-to-fill, and workforce satisfaction. Local clinicians should be involved in the planning and governance so that the plan reflects real field conditions and isn’t just a top-down exercise.

From personal experience, when services are understaffed or training pipelines are fitful, families feel the pressure most acutely. A year with adequate GP numbers meant fewer blocks in urgent care, better access to mental health support, and less scramble to find slots that fit a family’s needs. Conversely, staff burnout and high vacancy rates lead to longer waits and more avoidable complications.

Ultimately, this isn’t just about more bodies; it’s about smarter, supported, and sustainable workforce systems. With secure funding, robust training, clear progression, and sensible staffing models, we can protect patient safety, improve access, and give NHS teams in Wales the stability they need to deliver high-quality care day after day.

Any NHS workforce plan must prioritise safety alongside access. Safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models should sit at the heart of expanding services, ensuring we do not dilute care quality as demand grows. Plan the skill mix around patient need, with protected staffing in key areas such as urgent care, district nursing and mental health, and keep patients seeing the same GP or nurse where possible. In my experience, when cover relies heavily on short-term locums, handovers falter and patients face unnecessary delays.

Strong safety monitoring is essential: regular audits, incident reporting, and real-time dashboards that show staffing levels against patient acuity so problems are spotted early and acted on quickly. For retention, offer flexible hours, part-time roles, job-sharing and phased retirement to keep skilled staff in the system while creating pathways for newer colleagues. Support with childcare, proactive mental health services, and readily accessible wellbeing resources helps reduce burnout.

A local framework that couples safe staffing with career development and staff-driven planning will help recruit and retain a diverse workforce while maintaining high-quality, safe care and improving access overall.

I believe any NHS workforce plan should prioritise sustainable, well-funded career development that keeps experienced clinicians and supports new staff. That means clearly funded career pathways, protected CPD time, structured mentorship, and robust return-to-practice schemes. In practice, this could include paid CPD in all roles, a mentoring network across disciplines, and dedicated posts to help clinicians re-enter practice after breaks. Ring-fenced, multi-year funding is essential to expand training capacity, support GP practices and allied health professions, and reduce the disruption caused by short-term policy changes.

Second, invest in interoperable, secure IT systems with comprehensive staff training, while safeguarding non-digital options for patients who are digitally excluded. Streamline admin to free clinicians for patient care, but maintain alternative routes for appointment access.

Third, ensure safe staffing levels and wellbeing support, with flexible working options to improve retention across rural and urban settings. Local teams should have the autonomy to tailor workforce strategies to local needs, so services remain reliable.

A stable, well-funded, future-proof plan will deliver safer care today and sustain it for years.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise people first—ensuring enough, well-supported staff across primary, community and mental health services to deliver safe, high-quality care that fits local need. absolutely from my position as a pensioner living in England, and drawing on my experiences of trying to get timely GP and community health support, I think an NHS workforce plan must prioritise front-line capacity first and foremost, while building robust digital tools that actually help, not hinder, patient care. The private bit I want to see is investment in interoperable IT and secure systems, paired with thorough staff digital training, but with strong safeguards for those who are digitally excluded. The plan should deliver safe, high-quality care through people who feel properly supported and who have the tools to do their jobs well.

- Put more boots on the ground: recruit and retain GPs, district nurses, practice nurses, mental health professionals and allied health staff with realistic workloads and fair pay. Reliable locums must be available to cover gaps so patients aren’t bounced from pillar to pillar or left waiting weeks for a slot. This also means clear career routes and professional development so staff stay in the NHS rather than migrating elsewhere.

- Protect continuity of care: patients, especially those with long-standing conditions, benefit from seeing the same clinician who knows their history. The plan should ensure MDTs work in a way that supports the GP role, with clear accountability and easy reversion to the primary clinician if a case isn’t straightforward. That reduces duplicate tests, repeated questions, and delays in medicines or referrals.

- Interoperable IT and secure systems: we need a seamless, shared patient record across primary, community and mental health services. Real-time booking, triage, e-prescribing, and safe information exchange between professionals should be standard. Robust cyber security and data protection must be non-negotiable so staff can work confidently.

- Staff digital training, with safeguards for digitally excluded patients: invest in ongoing training so every member of staff can use new systems effectively. Appoint tech champions, provide user-friendly interfaces, and ensure IT support is readily available. Crucially, maintain non-digital pathways—phone lines with reliable triage, in-person appointments, and home visits—so those without digital access are not left behind.

- Practical, person-centred digital tools: the digital system should truly speed things up. Examples in practice would include integrated scheduling that flags urgent same-day slots, alerts for missed calls or follow-ups, and digital reminders that do not penalise patients who struggle with technology. But if a patient cannot use digital tools, there must be a straightforward alternative that is equally responsive.

- Support for the workforce beyond tech: more administrative and care-coordination staff to handle non-clinical tasks, freeing clinicians to see patients promptly. Adequate time for training, supervision and reflective practice helps prevent burnout and keeps care safe. An environment that looks after clinicians’ wellbeing supports better patient care too.

- Local flexibility with a national standard: while these priorities stay constant, staffing models should accommodate local needs—urban deprivation areas, rural communities, and pockets with older populations may require different mixes of staff and outreach support. Transport assistance and home-visit capacity are essential for those with mobility issues or who are housebound.

- Metrics and accountability: track vacancy and turnover rates, wait times for appointments, and patient safety indicators. Regular audits of MDT coordination and continuity of care should be part of the plan so we can see whether staffing changes actually improve access and outcomes.

In short, the workforce plan should deliver enough, well-supported clinicians who collaborate effectively through interoperable, secure digital systems, while preserving non-digital routes and practical support for digitally excluded patients. This combination offers safer, higher-quality care and more reliable access for people like me, who value a consistent clinician, clear appointment access, and care that doesn’t hinge on always being online.

From where I’m standing in England, any NHS workforce plan has to put people at the heart of care and make sure safety and quality aren’t sacrificed in pursuit of more hires or faster digital systems. A practical, well-funded plan should deliver both the recruitment to fill shortages and the support to keep staff delivering safe, compassionate care day in, day out.

Priorities for recruitment
- Targeted competitive pay and retention payments, plus relocation packages and bursaries, to attract staff to underserved areas and to high-demand roles such as district nurses, mental health professionals, and AHPs. Without meaningful financial incentives, there will be little reason for qualified people to move from where they are to more stretched parts of the country, especially if housing and cost of living are constraints.
- A deliberate, place-based approach. Invest in local pipelines—school and college outreach, hospitality-style internships in GP practices, and partnerships with universities to encourage students to train in roles that the local NHS badly needs. In my area we’ve heard of promising graduates leaving the first year after training because they can’t find a supportive team or secure stable hours.
- Clear career pathways that combine recruitment with progression. People won’t stay if there’s no visible future, so bursaries should come with guaranteed placements and mentor support that helps people move from student to practitioner to advanced clinician or supervisor.

Staff retention and safety in care delivery
- Safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models. I’m convinced care quality suffers when teams rotate constantly or rely heavily on agency staff. Keeping the same core team with predictable workloads helps patients build trust and enables staff to deliver higher-quality, safer care.
- Robust safety monitoring. Real-time dashboards that track staffing levels against patient outcomes, incident reports, and staff wellbeing indicators should drive adjustments quickly. For example, if headcount dips in a ward, the system should automatically flag risk and trigger proactive staffing refresh rather than waiting for a formal review.
- Minimise non-clinical burden and admin drag. Staff spend too much time on electronic forms, double-handovers, and chasing approvals. Better admin support, streamlined IT workflows, and smarter delegation would free clinicians to focus on patients, which is a real retention lever.

Flexible working to retain a diverse workforce
- Flexible hours, part-time options, job-share arrangements, and phased retirement. These must be normalised, not exceptional. For many, flexible patterns help manage caring responsibilities, health issues, or later-life careers, and they’re essential to broadening who can work in NHS roles.
- Comprehensive childcare and family support. On-site or partnered childcare, plus sabbatical-like break options for carers, can remove a major barrier to entering or staying in NHS roles.
- Proactive mental health and wellbeing services. Access to confidential, timely mental health support and regular wellbeing check-ins reduces burnout, keeps staff healthier, and sustains performance over the long term.

Education, training and progression
- Invested training budgets that fund apprenticeships and ongoing professional development. Practical, funded development keeps people engaged and builds skill depth in hospitals and community settings alike.
- Mentoring and protected time for learning. Staff should have dedicated time to train while maintaining safe patient coverage; that balance is essential to retention.

A practical delivery model that protects quality
- Hybrid approaches where digital tools help, not replace, human contact. Online triage, e-learning, and remote booking have benefits, but must be implemented alongside robust non-digital access and solid human support lines. The plan should explicitly fund hybrid options that cater to those less comfortable with tech or without reliable connectivity.
- Local hubs and continuity of care. Where possible, services should be organised to reduce handoffs and travel for patients—use team-based hubs that keep the same clinicians closer to the same cohorts of patients.

Evidence and accountability
- Publish clear staffing and safety metrics so patients can see that staffing levels meet evidence-based thresholds and that ongoing interventions actually reduce wait times and improve outcomes. This isn’t about name-and-shame; it’s about continuous improvement and public trust.

In short, the workforce plan must couple strong recruitment incentives with robust retention strategies, all calibrated to preserve and improve patient safety and care quality. It’s not enough to hire more bodies if we don’t also invest in the conditions, hours, and support systems that keep those staff well, engaged, and able to deliver the high standard of care people expect and deserve. If we fund and manage this right, the NHS can recruit effectively, retain a diverse and resilient workforce, and maintain high-quality care across communities.
