Fourth, invest in training capacity, practical placements, mentorship and wellbeing support to improve retention and morale, plus smarter rostering to reduce burnout. Finally, ensure robust governance and safety nets as teams expand, with clear accountability and quality assurance. This approach would support access and continuity while protecting patient safety.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise realistic, locally tailored recruitment and retention strategies that keep patients safe and high‑quality care achievable, especially in rural, coastal and urban deprived areas. From my observations around England, these places bear the brunt of long vacancies and intermittent GP and nursing cover. The plan should include targeted incentives: housing support or subsidies in high‑cost or hard‑to‑fill areas, transport assistance to reduce barriers for shifts outside normal hours, relocation grants, and clear career progression routes that local staff can access. For international recruitment, ensure rigorous induction, strong mentorship, and sustainable integration to avoid quick fixes that disrupt continuity.

Retention must go beyond pay. Offer flexible working patterns and predictable rosters, funded return‑to‑practice and career‑development programmes, and protected time for training and supervision. Strengthen local pipelines through student placements, apprenticeships, and ties with universities in rural and deprived areas to build a sustainable workforce. Improve wellbeing support, mental health resources, and manageable workloads to reduce burnout and turnover. Ensure safe staffing levels with reliable recruitment before service expansion, and use technology to support triage and team‑based care rather than overloading individuals. In a coastal town near me, vacancies have persisted for months, leading to longer waits and stressed teams—precisely the risk this plan must address with practical, area‑specific solutions.

I would like the NHS workforce plan to prioritise practical changes that translate into more time for patients and safer care. In practice this means reducing unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks, and streamlining referrals while improving IT usability and interoperability. When clinicians spend less time chasing forms and duplicating data, they can focus on actually diagnosing and supporting patients, especially in busy GP surgeries and community teams. 

Clarify scope-of-practice, revalidation, indemnity and fund protected clinical supervision to support new roles and maintain patient safety. Clear, supported pathways for roles like physician associates and advanced nurse practitioners reduce bottlenecks and expand access while keeping checks and balances. 

Secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlements to enable sustained workforce initiatives, training capacity and reduce short-term policy volatility. Local implementation benefits from predictable budgets that allow recruiting, training slots and wellbeing programmes without constant upheaval. 

In my local area, simplification of referral routes and a user-friendly IT system freed up time for patient care; protected supervision hours would help new clinicians gain confidence. A plan that also funds language skills and cultural competence as part of staffing would improve access for diverse communities, aligning with our goal of safe, high-quality care for all.

Thank you for asking a question that gets to the heart of what we need to deliver safe, high-quality care for patients now and into the future. My view remains that a credible NHS workforce plan must be built on real, sustainable capacity growth in the domestic supply of primary care and related services, underpinned by safety and continuity of care. With that in mind, I would prioritise the following:

- Expand the domestic supply chain for primary care staff
  - Increase undergraduate, postgraduate, and apprenticeship places across medicine, nursing, allied health, and pharmacy with protected clinical placements in primary care settings. Universities and practice networks should form lasting partnerships to ensure curricula reflect everyday primary care needs and the reality of team-based care. This must be backed by funded return-to-practice routes and well-designed bridging programmes so experienced professionals can rejoin the workforce safely.
  - Create clear career pathways that encourage progression into primary care roles, including nurse practitioners, physician associates, pharmacists with extended roles, and clinicians who can share responsibilities across GP practices. A pipeline that patients can see as long-term and stable will improve recruitment and retention more effectively than one-off incentives.

- Prioritise safe staffing and continuity of care
  - Establish safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models as core design principles of any workforce plan. Teams should be structured to reduce dependency on a single clinician and promote continuity of care through longer patient-clinician relationships or stable small teams.
  - Invest in multidisciplinary teams (practice-based pharmacists, mental health practitioners, physiotherapists, social care links) so workload is distributed and access remains timely even when individual staff are off sick or on leave.
  - Implement robust safety monitoring and governance, with real-time dashboards that track staffing levels, wait times, patient outcomes, and staff wellbeing metrics. Use that data to adjust recruitment, training, and rostering in a timely way rather than waiting for annual reviews.

- Secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding and predictable delivery models
  - Provide multi-year funding settlements that guarantee investment in training capacity, workforce planning, and reduced policy volatility. Ring-fencing money for education, supervision, and admin support helps practices plan with confidence and protects patient safety.
  - Allocate dedicated funding for protected placements, supervision, and time for clinicians to teach and mentor trainees. This should be paired with resources for administrative support so clinicians can spend more time with patients and less time on paperwork.
  - Ensure funding envelopes support flexible working without undermining training quality or continuity of care. This includes support for job-sharing, cross-site rotations, and part-time routes that enable a broader pool of talented people to stay in primary care.

- Strengthen retention and wellbeing as a core driver of quality
  - Prioritise workload management, admin burden reduction, and accessible occupational health and mental health services. Sufficient protected time for planning, professional development, and reflective practice is essential to prevent burnout and maintain high standards of care.
  - Link pay progression and career development to measurable improvements in patient access and safety, while avoiding a narrow focus on short-term incentives. Ensure remuneration reflects workload, living costs, and the value of primary care to the wider health system.

- Align international recruitment with domestic capacity building
  - Maintain a measured role for international recruitment but ensure it complements, rather than substitutes, a strong domestic training pipeline. When international staff join, provide structured induction, language and cultural support, and supervision to protect patient safety and support retention.

- Evaluation, governance and adaptability
  - Build in milestones and robust evaluation from the outset. Share learnings across regions, scale successful models, and be prepared to recalibrate in light of evidence. A plan that adapts to changing needs but remains anchored in sustainable capacity and patient safety is far more likely to deliver lasting improvements in access and quality.

In our networks, long-term workforce planning that combines training capacity expansion with flexible working, admin support, and safe staffing has yielded clearer improvements in access and morale. Short-term fixes or relying heavily on agency staff without addressing the root capacity gaps simply transfer risk, erode continuity and undermine safety. A credible NHS workforce plan must therefore commit to expanding domestic supply, safeguarding patient safety, and delivering stable, well-funded development paths for staff across primary care and community services.

I strongly support prioritising transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with clear evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding and performance monitoring. A workforce plan should start with dependable local data on vacancies, turnover, training needs and patient demand so we can forecast shortages before they bite and tailor recruitment pipelines from nearby universities and allied health education. Use predictive modelling to align staffing with projected activity, including peaks in urgent care and community services, and to plan for resilience during winter pressures. Fund the right mix of staff in the right places by linking resources to measurable outcomes: safe staffing levels, patient experience, wait times and clinical outcomes. Establish local dashboards that publicise vacancy rates, sickness absence and staff support metrics, and require periodic reviews to adjust funding. Implement clear career pathways, supervision and mentoring, flexible working, and well-being support to improve retention. Technology should support, not burden, clinicians: digital scheduling, cross-team referrals and data-sharing must be accompanied by training and governance to protect privacy. In practice, local workforce plans backed by transparent data can help maintain safe, high-quality care while expanding access and moving towards the reform goals I outlined earlier.

To recruit, retain and support staff while safeguarding safety and high-quality care, the plan must prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams to safely redistribute GP workload. Invest in formal MDTs that include nurses, nurse practitioners, GPs practice nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied roles, all operating within clear scopes and under robust supervision by senior clinicians. Build strong training pipelines with protected time for ongoing CPD, competency assessments and regular supervision so new and existing staff can develop without compromising safety. 

In practice, this means nurse-led chronic disease clinics for stable patients, pharmacist-led medicines reviews and deprescribing in polypharmacy, physician associates handling same-day triage and routine reviews, and paramedics doing targeted home visits for non-life-threatening cases. These teams should follow standardised protocols with rapid escalation pathways to GPs when complexities arise, plus regular audits and outcome dashboards to monitor safety and quality. 

Success relies on governance and fair, sustainable workforce measures: competitive pay, flexible hours, wellbeing and burnout safeguards, and modern rostering and digital booking systems that actually reduce backlog. Maintain rigorous recruitment standards, including international recruitment where appropriate, but with strong integration and supervision. This approach can lower GP workload, shorten waits, and preserve care quality for patients in all communities.

To recruit, retain and support staff while safeguarding safe, high‑quality care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise tailored incentives for hard‑to‑fill areas (rural, coastal, urban deprived), including housing assistance, transport subsidies or relocation grants, and targeted career pathways with local training partners. Retention depends on genuinely flexible working: part‑time and job‑share options, phased retirement, reliable childcare support, and proactive mental‑health services to mitigate burnout. In practice, offering flexible shifts that align with caring responsibilities and providing housing or travel support in remote communities makes roles sustainable and appealing. Local pilots that combine housing support with predictable rosters have shown improved uptake in our area. Strengthen safety and quality by coupling these measures with robust workforce planning, safe‑staffing metrics, ongoing professional development, mentoring and easy access to confidential wellbeing services. A hub model with integrated digital rostering will help balance demand across services and keep care coherent.

From my perspective living in England and seeing how the system trips up when staffing is thin, any NHS workforce plan must prioritise growing the workforce in a sustainable, safe, and well-supported way. It should not just aim to fill vacancies but to build capacity that matches the demand we’re already facing in primary care, community, and mental health, while protecting the quality and safety of care people rely on. I’d expect a plan to balance three core aims: grow the supply of capable staff, incentivise retention in hard-to-fill areas, and support international recruitment in a responsible way that strengthens health systems both here and abroad.

1) Grow domestic supply through education and training with protected placement time
- Increase undergraduate and postgraduate places across medical, nursing, allied health, and pharmacy streams, with protected placements that are ring-fenced for community and primary care settings. Partnerships between universities and NHS trusts should run joint training hubs where students rotate through GP practices, community clinics, and mental health teams without being pulled into service pressures elsewhere.
- Expand apprenticeship routes and formalised work-integrated learning so people can enter roles such as nursing associates, physician associate apprentices, and other allied health professionals while still under supervision. Protected time for clinical mentors and supervisors is essential to avoid overload.
- Develop regional training pathways that tie into local workforce needs, so new staff are more likely to stay in the areas that need them most. This also helps with career progression and creates a clearer ladder from learner to frontline clinician.
- Use real-time workforce forecasting to align training outputs with anticipated vacancies, rather than training to old demand levels. We’ve seen how a mismatch can leave new graduates with limited local opportunities—dead-end cycles help no one and risk driving away talent.

2) Target incentives for hard-to-fill areas – housing, transport, and flexible working
- Deliver tailored incentives for rural, urban-deprived, and coastal locations, including affordable housing schemes near practice bases, relocation support, and enhanced transport options. These areas are the ones most likely to lose people to larger cities if the package isn’t compelling.
- Provide flexible working patterns and safer staffing ratios that reduce burnout. For example, longer career pathways allowing gradual progression, protected time for training, and scheduler systems that prevent repeated after-hours spikes.
- Create regional “staff wellbeing nets”—easy access to mental health and wellbeing support, peer supervision, and clinical supervision for less-experienced staff in high-demand settings. Frontline staff need to feel their wellbeing is treated as a priority, not an afterthought.

3) Use overseas recruitment responsibly and ethically
- A streamlined visa and credential recognition process is important, but it must be paired with structured integration support: language and cultural orientation, locally relevant induction, and mentorship to help international staff settle into teams and communities.
- Maintain robust safeguards to prevent depleting source-country health systems and to ensure that international recruitment supplements rather than substitutes for domestic capacity. This includes fair employment terms, recognition of prior learning, and ongoing professional development.
- Set up welcome hubs and buddy schemes that pair newcomers with experienced local clinicians, so integration happens quickly and patients experience consistent, high-quality care.

4) Retention, development, and safety at the heart of the plan
- Invest in ongoing professional development and clear career ladders. Staff should see a long-term future in the NHS, not just a temporary stopgap. Dedicated funding for supervision, mentoring, and protected study time is essential.
- Ensure safe patient loads and staffing levels so clinicians can deliver care without compromising safety. This means robust workforce planning, dynamic rostering, and a culture where seeking help or pausing to prevent errors is supported.
- Improve data use: transparent, disaggregated data on recruitment, turnover, burnout, and patient outcomes. This helps target interventions where they’re needed most and track whether the plan is actually delivering safer, higher-quality care.

5) Co-design, phased implementation, and accountability
- Frontline staff and patients must be involved in shaping the plan from the start. Test approaches in stages, monitor for unintended bottlenecks, and adjust quickly rather than waiting for a high-stakes evaluation far down the line.
- Ensure sustainable funding streams that aren’t contingent on temporary incentives. Workforce initiatives that look good on a slide must translate into dependable staffing levels and real improvements in patient experience.

In short, a strong NHS workforce plan should grow domestic supply through university- and practice-linked training, tailor incentives to the areas most in need, recruit overseas workers in a way that respects source countries and supports integration, and place staff wellbeing and safe care at the core. When these pieces sit together, we’ll see shorter waits for patients, more stable teams, and a health service that can actually sustain the level of care people expect and deserve.

I welcome a NHS workforce plan that keeps people safe while making it easier to recruit and keep the staff we need. In practice, that means clear roles, steady development opportunities, flexible working, and robust protection for patients across primary, community, and mental health settings. The aim should be to grow a stable, well-supported workforce that can deliver timely, high-quality care without burning people out.

- Clarity on scope of practice, revalidation and indemnity: We need explicit, nationally consistent guidance on what each professional can do in each setting, with simple pathways to expand scopes where needed. Clear revalidation processes are essential so clinicians can stay up to date without unnecessary red tape. Indemnity arrangements must be predictable and publicly funded where new roles and expanded responsibilities are involved; otherwise, clinicians will be hesitant to take on expanded duties or adopt innovative models. For example, as teams take on more integrated work in co-located hubs, a pharmacist, an ANP, or a mental health practitioner may share tasks with GPs or district nurses—this only works if everyone is protected and properly supervised.

- Fund protected clinical supervision and professional development: New roles and expanded duties require ongoing supervision, mentorship and protected time for reflective practice. In our local hub, staff have benefited from supervision that helps them manage complex cases and reduces risk. If we want to sustain a multi-disciplinary approach, we must allocate dedicated time and funding for supervision, case reviews, and peer support, so patient safety is not compromised as teams evolve.

- Flexible working to recruit and retain a diverse workforce: Flexible hours, part-time options, job-sharing, phased retirement, and strong childcare support are not luxuries—they’re essential to retaining talented people who might otherwise leave due to caring responsibilities or burnout. For example, allowing a joint role where a district nurse and a community physio share responsibilities can keep experienced staff engaged while also opening pathways for career progression. Proactive mental health services and easier access to wellbeing resources should be standard, not optional.

- Safe staffing ratios and continuity of care: As we push for access improvements, we must not dilute clinical quality. Plan for safe staffing ratios across all critical services and prioritise continuity-preserving models—where patients see the same clinicians where possible—to maintain trust and safety. This means reducing reliance on ad hoc agency staff and using long-term rosters, so teams know each other’s routines and can recognise warning signs early.

- Cross-disciplinary training and governance: Staff should train to work across settings—GP clinics, community nursing, and mental health teams—so integration is not a barrier but a norm. Governance structures should monitor patient safety indicators, staff wellbeing, and workload alongside waiting times and access targets. Sharing data and learning from near-misses or safety concerns must be embedded in everyday practice, with clear actions and accountability.

- Targeted recruitment and retention for a diverse workforce: We should actively recruit from local communities and provide language support, culturally competent training, and accessible routes into practice. This includes robust induction, mentorship, and ongoing professional development to help newcomers grow confidence and stay in the system.

- Practical examples from the ground: In hubs already testing integrated care, patients benefit from faster triage, more same-week follow-ups, and a perception that care feels ‘joined up.’ However, staff sometimes report feeling stretched when vacancies aren’t filled promptly or when training and supervision aren’t funded. A sustainable plan would lock in funding for supervision, make indemnity costs predictable, and ensure managers have the tools to rotate staff safely without compromising service continuity.

Ultimately, the workforce plan should recognise that improving access is not just about more staff or longer hours; it’s about intelligent staffing, supportive leadership, and safeguarding patient safety at every step. By clarifying roles, investing in supervision, enabling flexible working, and maintaining safe, continuous care, we can recruit, retain and empower the NHS workforce to deliver timely, high-quality care for everyone.

absolutely ensuring safe, high-quality care hinges on a stable, well-supported NHS workforce. The plan should prioritise tailored incentives for hard-to-fill areas—rural, urban deprived and coastal—paired with housing and transport support so staff can relocate or commute without discouragement. This could include local relocation packages, affordable housing options, travel subsidies, flexible or extended contracts, clear career progression paths and targeted professional development to build local pipelines. 

Alongside recruitment, we must address retention through realistic workloads, adequate staffing levels, protected time for training, and robust wellbeing and occupational health support. Practical tools like efficient rosters, supportive supervision for clinicians, and access to mental health resources are essential to avoid burnout and maintain safety. 

Crucially, underpin all of this with transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks. Real-time dashboards, scenario planning and regular reviews can inform funding, recruitment campaigns and performance monitoring. Local workforce partnerships should own the plans and adapt them as demographics shift. In short: combine targeted, well-supported staffing strategies with strong data governance to deliver safer, higher-quality care!

To ensure recruitment, retention and safe, high-quality care, the NHS workforce plan must prioritise growing the domestic supply of primary care staff. This means increasing undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships. In Wales I’ve seen trainees struggle to secure placements in solid GP settings, and long waits for mentors undermine training capacity; protected placements would stabilise entry routes and improve retention by giving real career pathways.

Second, secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlements so training capacity and workforce initiatives aren’t at the mercy of short-term policy changes. Uncertainty makes staffing plans unreliable and delays essential improvements.

Third, clarify scope-of-practice, revalidation and indemnity arrangements while funding protected clinical supervision for new roles. Clear rules ensure patient safety as staff expand roles—like nurse practitioners, pharmacists, and physician associates in primary care—without ambiguity over liability or escalation. Regular, funded supervision helps new staff grow confidence and competence.

Together these steps will build resilience, reduce burnout, and deliver safer care for communities in Wales.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise three interlinked strands. First, tailored incentives for hard-to-fill areas—rural, urban deprived and coastal—plus housing and transport support to make posts viable long-term. This could include NHS accommodation near practices, relocation grants, subsidised travel and flexible rosters to fit family needs, which in my view would help reduce turnover. Second, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams: nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals working alongside GPs, with robust training and supervision to safely redistribute workload. In practice, a pharmacist-led chronic disease clinic in a GP practice, or a nurse practitioner co-managing visits, would ease pressure on GPs and improve continuity of care. Third, increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships. Local pipelines—students from local schools, funded foundation placements in primary care, and longer apprenticeships—would grow the domestic primary care workforce and support stable staffing in communities with transport barriers. In my experience, such integrated training and local recruitment reduce vacancy gaps and help patients access timely care, especially in underserved areas.

I think the NHS workforce plan should prioritise secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding to support sustained workforce initiatives, expand training capacity, and reduce short-term policy volatility. A stable budget base makes it possible to recruit and train new roles in primary and community care—pharmacists, physiotherapists, physician associates, mental health workers—without constant restructuring or abrupt cuts. It would also allow for larger, well-planned training pipelines and return-to-practice schemes so experienced staff aren’t lost to burnout or inactivity. In my area, where I’ve seen how a lack of capacity creates delays, a funded, longer-term plan would enable practices to staff embedded teams who can handle routine checks, minor injuries, and triage, freeing GPs for complex care. It’s essential to fund protected time for professional development, supervision, and flexible working to improve retention. Rural and underserved areas should have targeted incentives so services aren’t pulled to cities. Clear role boundaries and robust IT must accompany expansion to keep care safe and coordinated. Without stability, gains in access and quality won’t be sustainable.

From my perspective as a long-standing resident of England, a workforce plan for NHS services should prioritise long-term stability as well as recruitment. Secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlements are essential to build training capacity, reduce reliance on short-term pilots and give trusts confidence to plan staffing well into the next decade. This would support better GP and nursing training, expanded roles for physician associates and district nurses, and wellbeing and flexible working measures that help retention. 

Second, the plan must invest in interoperable, secure IT and staff digital training, so that information flows safely and referrals are faster across primary and community care. At the same time, safeguards are needed for digitally excluded patients, ensuring strong alternatives such as well-supported phone access, home visits, and in-person clinics. 

Practical steps I’ve seen work include protected admin time, stable budgets for locum cover where needed, clear career progression, and mentoring. When teams feel supported and IT works smoothly, care quality remains high and burnout falls, which is crucial for safe, sustainable NHS services.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. Any NHS workforce plan must be measured, well funded and people-centred. It should recruit, retain and support staff while preserving the safety and quality of care we rely on every day. To be effective in Scotland, the plan needs to balance digital transformation with robust alternatives for those who cannot or do not want to engage digitally, grow domestic capacity, and recruit responsibly from abroad. Here are priorities I believe matter most.

- Invest in interoperable, secure IT and boost staff digital competencies. A modern NHS needs a unified, privacy-protective digital backbone that works across primary care, community services and mental health. That means shared electronic patient records, reliable digital triage tools, and secure messaging between teams. Crucially, we must protect clinicians from constant system changes and data burdens by providing protected training time, clear governance, and user-friendly interfaces. Investment should be accompanied by real-world testing in diverse settings, including rural and urban clinics, to ensure solutions improve care rather than slow it down.

- Safeguard access for digitally excluded patients. Digital tools can improve speed and coordination, but they must not widen inequity. The plan should preserve and strengthen telephone and in‑person options, with digital inclusion pilots that link with community hubs, libraries, and social care. Provide digital literacy support, devices, and affordable connectivity where needed, plus simple options to switch between channels. In practice, a patient without reliable broadband should still get timely triage, appointments and follow‑ups without having to navigate a complex online labyrinth.

- Increase domestic capacity with protected training placements. Expand undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places for primary care and allied health roles, anchored by university-practice partnerships and protected placements in frontline settings. This includes GP training, nurse prescribers, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, and mental health workers. Key features should be durable funding, clear progression routes, and a workforce planning framework that prioritises high-need areas and rural/remote communities to avoid simply moving shortages around.

- Promote responsible overseas recruitment. If used, it should be deliberate and ethical: streamlined visa routes, recognition of credentials, structured integration support, language and cultural competence training, and robust safeguards against undermining health systems in source countries. Recruitment should be coupled with local capacity building so the overall system strengthens, not drains, global health. Any international recruitment must be transparently reported and matched to genuine domestic deficits rather than quick fixes.

- Strengthen retention through workload management and wellbeing. Safe, high‑quality care starts with sustainable staffing. That means evidence-based rostering, appropriate skill mix, and flexible working where possible to reduce burnout. Support for supervision, continuing professional development, mentorship, and leadership pathways should be integral, not optional. A healthy workplace culture, with clear escalation pathways and mental health support, is essential to attract and keep skilled staff.

- Embed governance, data and evaluation. The workforce plan should rely on real-time dashboards showing staffing levels, wait times, turnover, training uptake, and patient outcomes. Regular evaluation, independent oversight and co-design with front-line teams will help adjust targets, prevent unintended consequences and maintain public trust.

- Coordinate with wider system reform. Workforce planning must align with service design, including extended access models, integrated mental health pathways, and strengthened community teams. Training and recruitment should be linked to these service designs so new staff are prepared for the actual work environment and can deliver the integrated care our communities need.

In summary, I would like to see a workforce plan that (1) accelerates secure, interoperable digital systems while preserving non-digital routes; (2) grows domestic capacity through committed training pipelines and partnerships; (3) recruits overseas only under strict safeguards and linked to domestic need; (4) prioritises staff wellbeing and safe staffing; and (5) uses rigorous data to guide implementation and continual improvement. With stable, long‑term funding and inclusive governance, such a plan can recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care across Scotland.

i really think thank you for asking. From my perspective living in England and dealing with busy local services, the NHS workforce plan must both grow capacity and protect the quality and continuity of care I’ve described before. A patient-focused, sustainable approach means welcoming skilled staff from overseas responsibly while also reducing unnecessary admin that eats into time with patients. The plan should prioritise a set of practical, implementable steps that keep patients safe and improve how care is coordinated across services.

Key priorities I would like to see:

- Ethical overseas recruitment with streamlined visas and credential recognition. We need a clear path for qualified clinicians from abroad to work here quickly, with proper language and cultural orientation and structured mentoring. Importantly, these arrangements must come with safeguards to avoid depleting health systems in other countries and with commitments to training and capacity-building there as well as in the UK. A guaranteed return or service obligation, plus investment in local training, would help balance the international recruitment.

- Build local capacity alongside international recruitment. Expand training posts for GPs, nurses, allied health professionals and mental health staff; create strong career pathways and flexible working patterns to improve retention. In our area, staff networks and mentoring have done a great deal to keep people engaged, and a plan that recognises and supports career development would help staff feel valued and stay long term.

- Reduce unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks. A lot of clinician time is lost to admin and repeated data entry. Streamlining referrals, standardising triage, and improving IT usability would free clinicians to spend more time with patients and less time chasing paperwork. This aligns with the longer, more thorough consultations I’ve argued for, particularly for people with complex needs.

- Invest in safe, well-supported teams and multidisciplinary care. More pharmacists, physiotherapists, social prescribers and mental health professionals working alongside GPs can share the load and provide more holistic care. When teams are properly resourced, a named clinician can coordinate a patient’s care across GP, community services and mental health services, which improves continuity and outcomes.

- Improve IT and digital workflows. Interoperable, user-friendly IT systems that support streamlined referrals, real-time sharing of care plans, and decision-support tools would save time and reduce errors. Clinicians shouldn’t have to navigate clunky systems to get basic information across services; a well-designed platform would make communication and follow-up straightforward for patients too.

- Focus on staff wellbeing, safety and reasonable workloads. The plan must guarantee appropriate staffing levels, protected time for training and supervision, and accessible mental health support for staff. When staff feel supported and workloads are manageable, patient safety and care continuity improve.

- Transparent, actionable metrics. The workforce plan should include clear indicators on safe staffing, wait times, staff burnout, training completion and patient outcomes, with regular public reporting so policies can be adjusted quickly if problems emerge.

If these features are in place, we can responsibly expand the NHS workforce without sacrificing the continuity of care that patients need. International recruitment can be a valuable part of the solution, but it must go hand in hand with a strong local pipeline, reduced admin burden, and better IT that frees clinicians to focus on patients. That combination would help us keep long-term relationships with patients while meeting rising demand, and it would preserve the high standard of care that families in our area rely on. Thank you for considering these priorities as you shape the plan.

I strongly believe that an NHS workforce plan should prioritise stability, clear career progression, and robust support for staff at every level, all while keeping patient safety at the heart of care. My own experience balancing work with family health needs makes me value predictable, well-supported teams. When staffing is stable and staff feel invested in, patients get safer, more thorough care, and the care system runs more smoothly.

First, secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlements. Short-term funding cycles create unpredictable recruitment plans and means trusts can’t commit to long-term workforce strategies. With predictable budgets, NHS organisations can implement sustained recruitment drives, expand training capacity, and invest in retention initiatives without constant policy volatility. For example, if a trust knows it has funding for GP and nursing trainee numbers over five years, they can build robust pipelines, offer structured rotations, and reduce reliance on temporary staffing.

Second, provide clear, funded career pathways. Staff need to see how they can progress, specialise, and contribute meaningfully over time. A plan should fund the whole ladder—from graduate entry roles through to advanced practice and leadership roles—without crippling step-jumps in pay or training requirements. Practically, this means protected time for courses, structured rotations between primary and community services, and formal recognition of expanded roles in pay bands where appropriate. When junior clinicians can map a realistic route to higher responsibilities, turnover drops and morale improves.

Third, protect CPD and provide mentoring. Continuing professional development is essential to keep skills current in a fast-changing landscape. Plans should guarantee funded CPD time, access to high-quality online and in-person courses, and dedicated study leave. Mentorship schemes should be embedded from early on—experienced clinicians guiding new entrants reduces uncertainty and promotes safe practice. In my conversations with colleagues, well-supported mentoring makes a tangible difference to confidence and retention, especially for those transitioning from training into frontline roles.

Fourth, expand return-to-practice and flexible-working pathways. People pause careers for family or caring responsibilities; returning with confidence requires targeted, funded routes, refresher modules, and flexible scheduling. Return-to-practice schemes should be straightforward to navigate, with bridging updates to align with current guidelines. Such pathways not only bring skilled clinicians back but also demonstrate to staff that the system values long-term contributions, not just initial recruitment.

Fifth, prioritise wellbeing, safe staffing, and manageable workloads. A plan that merely hires more staff without addressing workload balance risks burnout and attrition. Invest in wellbeing supports, supervisory capacity, and safe staffing levels that reflect patient needs. Flexible working patterns and predictable rosters help staff balance life and work, which in turn supports better patient safety and higher-quality care.

Finally, anchor workforce planning in data and local needs. Use local demand modelling to align training placements and rotations with the most pressing gaps—whether in general practice, community health, or mental health services. Strong, data-driven planning ensures the right mix of skills in the right places at the right times, improving access and reducing avoidable risks.

In short, an NHS workforce plan should deliver stable, long-term funding; transparent, funded career ladders; protected CPD with mentoring; robust return-to-practice routes; and practical wellbeing and safe-staffing supports. When staff feel supported and have a clear path forward, high-quality, safe care becomes more feasible even as demand grows. Do not let digital upgrades come at the expense of those who need a face‑to‑face appointment or a longer, careful assessment.
- Proactive workforce planning and data use: Use predictive analytics to forecast demand by area (urban, rural, coastal) and model different staffing scenarios. Planning must align with training capacity, local recruitment, and the roll‑out of new models of care, so the system isn’t surprised by seasonal spikes or demographic shifts.
- Quality and patient experience as the test: Staffing plans should tie to measurable outcomes—hospital admission rates from primary care, patient satisfaction, and equity of access. If changes to staffing or models compromise quality, the plan should be revised, not doubled down.

In short, a strong NHS workforce plan should safeguard safe care while expanding access, not treat them as opposing goals. By prioritising safe, well‑supported staff, maintaining continuity of care, and investing in interoperable tech and targeted training—with safeguards for digitally excluded patients—we can recruit and retain capable staff without sacrificing the high standards patients expect. Personal experience with busy clinics and remote or telehealth options shows that when staff aren’t stretched to breaking point and systems work smoothly, access improves and care quality follows.

The plan should prioritise a dual approach: immediate, targeted incentives to attract people into high‑demand roles and underserved areas, and secure, long‑term funding to sustain training and retention. Competitive pay for frontline staff, retention payments for experienced clinicians, relocation packages and bursaries for students and returners are essential to fill vacancies quickly and reduce unsafe workloads. In my area, vacancies linger when there aren’t attractive packages to move people here or to stay long term, which feeds pressure on the whole system.

To deliver timely, safe care we need an NHS workforce plan that puts people at its heart and builds from there. First, prioritise clear, funded career pathways, protected continuing professional development, strong mentorship and return‑to‑practice schemes to retain experienced clinicians and support early‑career staff. In my area we rely on a steady mix of GP and mental health professionals; without dedicated time and progression opportunities, skilled staff leave for better packages elsewhere. Concrete steps could include funded leadership time for supervisors, structured return‑to‑practice routes after career breaks, and protected CPD slots that align with service needs. 

Second, cut unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks, and streamline referrals while improving IT usability to free clinician time for patients. We need simpler, integrated IT and digital referral systems so a person is seen promptly rather than stuck in admin loops. My experience of a family member waiting months for CBT after referral shows how admin burden and fragmented IT slow care and risk deterioration.

Third, develop transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding and performance monitoring. Local dashboards that track staffing, wait times and outcomes will help direct resources where they are most needed and enable real, accountable improvement.

I believe an NHS workforce plan should prioritise safe, high-quality care while making it feasible to recruit, retain and support staff, especially in rural Wales. Clarity around scope-of-practice for evolving roles—nurse prescribers, paramedics with extended duties, physician associates—with straightforward governance helps teams work cohesively and prevents duplication or gaps. Revalidation and ongoing professional development must be funded and protected; clinicians need dedicated time to refresh skills and adopt new care models without always chasing patients. Indemnity arrangements must be clear, affordable and predictable for staff taking on new responsibilities, so fear of liability doesn’t hold back improvements in local services. The plan should also fund protected clinical supervision and protected time for mentoring, peer review and case-based learning, which is vital in rural areas where specialist support is thinner. In my experience in village care, strong supervision and clear roles keep patient safety high even when staff numbers fluctuate. Recruitment and retention require regionally tailored packages, flexible working options, clear career progression, and local leadership opportunities within teams. Finally, maintain multidisciplinary, well-governed teams with clear pathways, and ensure non-digital access remains for those who prefer it, so safety isn’t compromised by technology gaps.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while keeping care safe and high quality, I think the workforce plan should focus on three linked priorities. First, strengthen links and joint funding with social care, mental health and community services. Co-funded, integrated teams can spread workload more evenly, with shared care plans and local hubs where GPs hand over to nurse practitioners, therapists and social workers. This would improve holistic care and prevent crises that lead to hospital admission, especially for older patients with multiple conditions. Second, expand training capacity in the domestic pipeline. Increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places, with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships so new staff are ready for primary care in our towns and villages. This should be supported by dedicated training posts in practices and community clinics. Third, cut admin and streamline processes. Reduce unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks; simplify referrals and improve IT usability and interoperability between systems. Provide better admin support and smarter digital tools so clinicians have more time for patients, not forms. In rural areas and towns alike, these steps would help maintain safe, high-quality care as the workforce grows and ages in our communities.

I think any NHS workforce plan worth its name must do two things at once: attract new staff into high‑demand roles and keep the people already delivering care, while ensuring safety and quality don’t get squeezed in the process. For someone like me, who is aware of how burnout and rigid shifts can push people out of the NHS, the plan should normalise flexible working and robust wellbeing support without compromising safe staffing levels or patient outcomes. Here are the priorities I’d push for.

- Flexible, diverse working arrangements to recruit and retain staff
  - Make flexible hours, part‑time roles, and job‑share options the norm rather than the exception. Provide clear career ladders for part‑time staff so progression doesn’t stall. A phased retirement path could help retain experienced clinicians while opening opportunities for younger colleagues.
  - Extend childcare support and family-friendly policies. On‑site nurseries or subsidised childcare, predictable rotas, and advance notice of shifts would make it much easier for staff with caring responsibilities to stay in the workforce.
  - Proactive mental health and wellbeing services, with easy access to confidential support and protected time for staff to use them. In my circle, burnout is not theoretical; it’s a day‑to‑day reality for colleagues juggling long shifts and exams or parental duties.

- Safety and continuity must be protected as access expands
  - Prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving rosters. When patient care is spread too thin or constantly handed off between teams, quality and safety suffer. Named, stable teams and consistent supervision help clinicians do their job well and patients receive safer care.
  - Implement robust safety monitoring and governance. Regular audits, transparent incident reporting, and rapid learning from near misses should be built into workforce planning so safety is not an afterthought when volumes rise.
  - Minimise unnecessary admin that drains clinical time. Streamlined IT, smarter triage, and more support staff for booking and care navigation free up clinicians to focus on direct patient care, which protects quality while expanding access.

- Attractive, targeted pay and incentives to move staff to high‑demand roles and areas
  - Competitive pay remains essential, but it should be complemented by retention payments, relocation packages, and bursaries or student loan write‑offs for working in underserved areas or in hard‑to‑fill specialisms.
  - Clear return‑to‑practice routes and funding for bridging courses would help people who paused their careers to rejoin with up‑to‑date skills.
  - Local and regional recruitment campaigns linked to housing support, schooling options, and welcoming local communities can make long‑term moves more feasible.

- Training, development and leadership opportunities
  - Funded CPD, apprenticeships, and structured supervision/mentorship are vital to keep staff engaged and up to date with best practice. A pathway from frontline clinician to team lead or service manager helps retain ambitious staff.
  - Create a pipeline that blends clinical work with leadership development, so experienced clinicians can shape safer, high‑quality services rather than leaving the front line for administrative roles.

- A practical approach to local workforce planning
  - Use data to forecast demand at local levels and tailor recruitment drives accordingly. In practice, that means partnerships with universities, schools, and local employers to build a steady stream of applicants for nursing, allied health, and GP roles.
  - Encourage rotational placements between primary, community, and hospital settings to build a versatile workforce comfortable with different care environments and patient needs.

In short, the plan should value people as much as outcomes. Flexible working and wellbeing must be embedded in the workforce model, but never in a way that undermines staffing safety or patient care. With safer rostering, clear career paths, and targeted financial incentives, we can attract talent to NHS roles, retain diverse staff, and maintain high‑quality care even as demand grows. Evidence from local trusts already shows that flexible staffing, good supervision, and supportive wellbeing services correlate with lower sickness absence and greater staff satisfaction—outcomes that translate directly into better patient access and safety. If the plan integrates these elements in a coherent, adequately funded way, we’ll not only fill vacancies but also build a resilient NHS workforce for the long term.

i really think as someone in England who has seen the day-to-day impact of staff shortages on access to GPs and mental health help, I believe any NHS workforce plan must be built around stability, clarity and real support for people delivering care. In practice, that means prioritising secure, multi-year, ring-fenced funding so workforce initiatives, training capacity and reductions in policy volatility aren’t knocked off course mid-stream by short-term budgets or political change. Short-term tinkering doesn’t fix the underlying problems; long-term certainty does. 

Key priorities I’d want to see in an NHS workforce plan
- Long-term, protected funding for training and workforce growth: Commit to multi-year funding for training posts in primary care, nursing, mental health, and allied health professionals. The plan should spell out how many training places are added each year, where they’ll be located (including rural and coastal areas), and when those new roles will be available locally. Without ring-fenced funding, local health economies will be forced to compete for resources, slowing progress and eroding confidence.
- Clear scope-of-practice, revalidation and indemnity arrangements: As new roles develop—such as extended-scope nurse practitioners, physician associates or clinical pharmacists—the plan should define their scope clearly to avoid confusion and ensure patient safety. Revalidation processes must be predictable and supportive, not a barrier to career progression. Indemnity arrangements should be aligned with the scope of practice so that staff aren’t caught by unexpected costs or complicated approvals when they’re trying to help patients who need timely care.
- Protected supervision and funded clinical supervision: Staff, especially those in training or newly expanded roles, need consistent mentorship and supervision. Fund protected time for senior clinicians to supervise, support professional development, and ensure patient safety isn’t compromised as teams grow. In my experience, where supervision is robust, new staff feel confident to work more independently without risking patient safety.
- Flexible, sustainable career paths and return-to-practice routes: The NHS should fund flexible routes into and back into clinical roles—back-to-practice schemes, apprenticeships in clinical settings, and supported retraining pathways. People pause their healthcare careers for family or other reasons; predictable, well-funded routes back to practice help maintain workforce numbers and preserve expertise.
- Focus on primary care and early-intervention mental health capacity: A credible plan must keep primary care at the core, expanding GP training and nurse-led clinics, as well as community therapies and stepped-care options, so people don’t drift into crisis. My own experience of waiting months for counselling is a stark reminder that without a robust pipeline for mental health staff, delays escalate problems and anxiety among students around exams and housing stress.
- Equity and geographic balance: Funding and training expansions should be distributed to reduce urban concentration. Rural and coastal areas often face the most acute shortages; the plan should include incentives and targeted recruitment from local communities to ensure every region can recruit and retain high-quality staff.
- Workforce planning with measurable milestones: A transparent timetable is crucial. Local authorities and NHS bodies need to publish annual targets for new posts, training capacity, and supervision commitments, plus progress against patient-safety metrics and staffing ratios. This visibility helps communities like mine feel confident that improvements aren’t empty promises.
- Integration with digital access and safe patient pathways: Use digital tools to improve scheduling and triage, but protect access channels for people who rely on phone or in-person support. A plan should specify how digital solutions will be deployed without leaving behind those with limited connectivity or skills.

Concrete examples informed by experience
- In campus and student clinics I’ve seen limited GP slots during exam periods create real stress. A workforce plan that prioritizes protected GP training slots, extended hours with safe staffing models, and nurse-led clinics could give students timely access without compromising care in other areas.
- In mental health, the bottleneck isn’t just awareness; it’s capacity. Ring-fenced funding to expand trainee numbers in CAMHS and community therapies, plus robust supervision, would help reduce the current multimonth waits for therapists and counsellors—which often spirals anxiety and risk in young people nearing critical deadlines.

Conclusion
A credible NHS workforce plan must balance immediate improvements with a stable, long-term strategy. Multi-year, ring-fenced funding, clear scope and revalidation systems, funded supervision, and equitable distribution are the bedrock for recruiting, retaining and supporting staff while maintaining high-quality care. If we get the governance right—transparent milestones, accountable delivery and patient-safety focused supervision—we can build a resilient workforce that delivers timely GP access, effective mental health support, and sustainable care for communities now and in the years ahead!

From where I’m standing in Wales, any NHS workforce plan needs to do more than just fill vacancies; it should secure the backing we need to deliver safe, high-quality care consistently, and it should do so in a way that matches the realities of communities like mine. I’m supportive of a multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlement. Short-term funding cycles create churn: projects start, then stall, staff training gets rolled back, and trusts end up running on priorities that change with the political wind. If we want sustainable improvements—especially in areas with higher demand or where language and cultural barriers add to difficulty—planning across several years is essential. That stability would let NHS organisations plan recruitment, training, and outreach at scale, rather than constantly firefighting the next budget squeeze. In practice, this could mean committing to a five-year plan for nurse and therapist training pipelines, with dedicated funds for apprenticeship routes and career progression, so someone can see a realistic path from student to clinician in our region.

Alongside funding stability, I’d prioritise investment in interoperable IT and secure systems, paired with comprehensive digital training for staff. My experience during recent years showed both the potential and the limits of digital health: online booking, instant messaging with clinics, and shared records can shave days off waiting times when used well, but only if systems talk to each other and security is solid. We need a backbone where GP practices, hospitals, and mental health services share information safely, so a clinician in a community centre can access a patient’s history and care plan without hours of paperwork. It’s crucial to keep options for digitally excluded patients—phone triage with trained operators, easier in-person help at local hubs, and translators when needed. I’ve seen friends struggle with digital-only systems where language or access barriers lock people out; that’s exactly what must be prevented. Training should cover not just how to use the tools, but how to explain them clearly to patients, including plain language and Welsh-language options so patients feel confident and understood.

We also need to offer targeted pay and recruitment incentives that address real gaps, particularly in underserved areas and high-demand roles. Competitive pay, retention payments, and relocation packages can make a real difference for someone choosing to move to rural or-border communities in Wales where recruitment is tougher. Bursaries for students from local communities who commit to a period of service in the NHS after qualification would build a workforce that reflects the people it serves. I’ve noticed that when staff feel valued and financially supported, they stay longer, perform better, and build trust with the patients who need them most. It’s not just about getting people in the door; it’s about giving them a viable, sustainable career with meaningful progression, safeguarding time for CPD and mentorship, and the chance to specialize in areas with the greatest local need.

A strong workforce plan should also ensure a steady pipeline into underserved areas through partnerships with schools, colleges, and universities here in Wales. More placements for nursing and allied health students in community and primary care teams, plus guaranteed access to training posts in local services, would help nurture a workforce that understands local health challenges—from language and cultural needs to the social determinants that hit hard in our communities. And while we push for digital transformation, we must keep staff and patients at the centre—systems should reduce administrative burdens, but not at the expense of human contact. Flexible working, decent staffing levels, and robust wellbeing support are non-negotiables if we want people to stay in the NHS and avoid burnout.

Finally, transparency matters. I’d want progress to be tracked and reported publicly, with clear, funded plans to address any gaps in access or outcomes by area or demographic group. If a particular community is lagging, there should be a concrete, funded response rather than excuses. Overall, the plan should blend funding certainty, smart technology, fair incentives, and strong links to local communities so that safe, high-quality care isn’t a wish but a lived reality for people in Wales and across the UK.

From my perspective in England, a NHS workforce plan that truly supports recruitment, retention and safe high-quality care needs to be practical, clearly mapped and funded for the long term. It should recognise that the right mix of skilled staff, with well-defined scope and robust support, is what keeps patients safe and services sustainable. In practice that means four core priorities: clear scope-of-practice and governance, reinforced professional development with protections for supervision, reliable indemnity arrangements, and sustainable staffing with staff wellbeing at the centre.

First, clarify scope-of-practice and governance for all roles, especially newer or expanding roles such as physician associates, advanced nurse practitioners, and clinical pharmacists working in primary and community care. This isn’t about limiting ambition; it’s about removing ambiguity that can lead to risky practice or unwarranted delays. The workforce plan should specify what tasks each role can perform, what must be supervised, and when a referral or escalation is required. It also needs a governance framework with regular audits and a clear pathway for accountability. When staff know their boundaries and can work to well-defined protocols, patient safety improves and confidence in services grows.

Second, ensure robust revalidation and protected continuing professional development (CPD). Professionals should have structured, funded time for learning and revalidation, integrated into service rotas so it does not become a burden on already stretched teams. In our practice, staff who have regular protected time to refresh knowledge—through shared training days, case reviews, and simulation where relevant—report fewer uncertainties in decision-making and better adherence to evidence-based care. A proactive plan would align CPD with local population needs, enabling skills to keep pace with new guidelines and technologies.

Third, establish reliable indemnity arrangements. Every member of staff delivering clinical care must be confident that they are adequately indemnified. A single, clear framework that applies across professions and new roles—whether GP partners, nurses, pharmacists, or allied health professionals—reduces risk for individuals and the organisation. This should come with transparent processes for obtaining and renewing indemnity, simple guidance for staff, and a mechanism to cover expanded scopes of practice as roles evolve.

Fourth, fund protected clinical supervision to support new roles and maintain patient safety. Safe delegation and senior oversight are not optional extras; they are essential for quality care as the workforce evolves. This means allocating time and resources for regular supervision, mentorship and reflective practice, with supervisors who have protected caseloads and up-to-date clinical governance training. In local teams, where a pharmacist prescriber or advanced nurse practitioner has weekly or bi-weekly supervised sessions with a clinician lead, there is better triage, more appropriate prioritisation of cases, and stronger antibiotic stewardship. Protected supervision should be standard, not an add-on funded only when there are spare funds.

Beyond these four pillars, I’d emphasise sustainable staffing models, staff wellbeing, and career progression. The plan should:
- Support effective recruitment and onboarding, including streamlined recruitment pipelines and return-to-practice pathways for those who’ve taken time away.
- Promote flexible and supportive working patterns to improve retention, without compromising safety.
- Use data dashboards to monitor skill mix, safe staffing levels, experience gaps, and training uptake so actions can be targeted where they’re most needed.
- Involve staff, and where possible patients and communities, in designing roles and pathways so they fit local needs and cultural contexts.

If the NHS commits to these priorities with stable, long-term funding and clear accountability, we’ll see safer care, better access, and a more resilient system. Staff will feel valued and capable, patients will experience more consistent quality, and local services won’t have to improvise under pressure.

I welcome the aim of a NHS workforce plan that keeps patient safety and high-quality care at the heart of it. From what I see in practice, the biggest barrier to good care isn’t just how many staff we have, but how they’re supported to do the right things with the right time and the right tools. A workforce plan needs to reduce needless targets and admin, clarify what people are allowed to do, and back new roles with proper supervision and funding. Here is how I think it should be prioritised:

- Cut the administrative burden and unused targets. We can’t keep piling more paperwork on clinicians. Streamline or remove duplicative targets, simplify recording requirements, and ensure that what’s asked of staff translates into real patient benefit. Use simpler, consistent documentation that travels across primary, community and mental health services so a clinician doesn’t have to re-enter the same information multiple times.

- Streamline referrals and improve IT usability. Referral pathways should be seamless between GP, community teams and hospitals. Interoperable IT systems, fewer logins, intuitive interfaces, and better decision-support would save hours that are currently spent chasing paperwork and duplicated steps. In practice, a busy nurse or GP ends up spending precious minutes on portals rather than talking with patients.

- Clarify scope-of-practice, revalidation and indemnity. We need clear, safe boundaries for what different roles can do—especially for newer roles like physician associates, advanced nurse practitioners and integrated pharmacists. Revalidation processes must be fit for purpose and not create cliff-edge barriers to workforce progression. Indemnity arrangements should be robust and consistent so staff can work with confidence and patients are protected.

- Fund protected clinical supervision and safe development of new roles. As new teams form, clinicians and allied health professionals benefit from dedicated supervision and mentoring. Allocate protected time for supervision, case reviews and ongoing training, not just annual appraisals. This also helps with patient safety when roles are expanding and day-to-day practice evolves.

- Invest in targeted recruitment and retention with decent working conditions. Address staffing shortages by offering flexible working, reasonable rosters, and support for those with caring responsibilities. Frontline staff are more likely to stay if they feel valued, supported and able to deliver care without constant firefighting against admin.

- Build multidisciplinary, community-facing teams. Strong teams that include care coordinators, social prescribers, and culturally competent staff help navigate patients through complex systems and reduce unnecessary hospital admissions. These roles must be properly funded and clearly integrated into the clinical workflow to avoid becoming “add-on” bureaucracy.

- Support IT-enabled patient-facing care. Where possible, offer online but also human-assisted access to information, with simple appointment booking, clear reminders, and help for those less comfortable with technology. In practice, that keeps more clinical time free for direct patient contact and reassurance, especially for older patients who need careful, respectful communication.

- Ensure data informs improvement without stigmatising areas with high need. The workforce plan should include data on workforce mix, workload, safety indicators and patient experience, but avoid a culture of ticking boxes. Use disaggregated data to spot where staff are stretched and where support is most needed, and then act locally to address gaps.

From where I sit, these changes would help clinicians do what they trained to do: care for people safely and with dignity, rather than chase forms or fight with clunky systems. In our area, I’ve seen how good interpreters, culturally aware staff, and practical support roles make a real difference to whether people engage with care. A plan that backs those elements with sensible, workload-friendly policies will help maintain safe, high-quality care for everyone.

To keep NHS services safe and high-quality while expanding capacity, the workforce plan should prioritise three things. First, clarify scope-of-practice across professions, ensure robust revalidation processes and fund protected clinical supervision for those taking on new roles. In my experience, when nurses or allied professionals expand their scope, without clear boundaries and mentoring, mistakes happen or confidence dips. Second, strengthen the links and joint funding with social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workload and enable more holistic care. Co-funded training, shared digital records, and closer teamwork could mean fewer handoffs and quicker care for patients with complex needs. In my area, people with long-term conditions often have to repeat information to multiple teams; better integration would help.

Third, for hard-to-fill roles and underserved areas, implement targeted pay and retention packages—competitive salaries, retention bonuses, relocation support, and bursaries for students. This is essential where GP and district nursing cover is thin. But this must be balanced with safe supervision, not just cash. Nurturing career paths, clear progression and protections will keep skilled staff in the NHS and protect patients.

From my perspective in Northern Ireland, any NHS workforce plan must be anchored in solid, locally meaningful data and clear accountability. Without that, decisions will miss where bottlenecks really lie and risk repeating the same mistakes. KPIs should cover patient safety, continuity of care, appointment availability, wait times and staff wellbeing, not just headcount. 

We need realistic modelling that tests how additional GP hours, nurse and allied health professional expansion, and new roles fit together without fragmenting care or shifting burdens elsewhere. Funding must be tied to tangible improvements in access and outcomes, with guaranteed local leadership and flexibility to respond to practice-specific needs. 

In practice, I’ve seen how the bottleneck is often the way we schedule and allocate ongoing care, not simply the number of staff. A plan that guarantees sustainable recruitment and retention—through predictable rosters, professional development, mentorship and manageable workloads—while being evaluated against transparent data, will protect continuity and safety. It needs to be locally led, with clear milestones and independent review to ensure we’re delivering high‑quality care, not just bigger teams.

A strong pipeline is needed too: more training posts, apprenticeships, supervision and wellbeing services, plus flexible working and protected admin time to reduce burnout. I think an NHS workforce plan should be clear about how to recruit, retain and support staff while making sure the care people receive remains safe and high‑quality. Key priorities should be: safe staffing, continuity of care, and strong safety monitoring, all integrated with social care and community services so work isn’t piled up in one corner of the system.

- Prioritise safe staffing ratios and predictable rosters
People don’t get timely, good care if teams are stretched beyond what a shift can safely handle. A plan should set clear minimum staffing levels for GP practices, community health teams and mental health services, with flexible rosters to cover absences without rushing patients through. This includes enough trained nurses, allied health professionals and support staff to handle triage, follow‑ups and preventative care. In practice, that means better recruitment pipelines, but also better retention—wellbeing support, reasonable hours, safe supervision and manageable workloads are essential so staff don’t burn out and drift away.

- Build continuity-preserving care models
Continuity matters, especially for young adults juggling exams, work, and mental health challenges. A workforce plan should promote named clinicians and stable teams, so patients are not shuffled with every appointment. Longer appointment times for complex needs and structured care plans that travel with the patient across services (GPs, mental health, social care) can improve outcomes and reduce repeat visits. Digital tools can help maintain continuity, such as a shared care record and a simple way to flag when a patient needs a follow‑up after a triage call.

- Strengthen safety monitoring and governance
Improvements in access must not come at the expense of safety. The plan should include robust safety monitoring—transparent dashboards on wait times, appointment lengths, incident reports, and patient feedback. Regular audits, risk assessments for home visits or outreach clinics, and clear escalation paths when capacity is strained will help keep quality up even as the system expands access.

- Integrate with social care and community services
One of the biggest wins is redistribution of workload across health and care sectors. The plan should promote joint funding and integrated teams that span primary care, social care, mental health and community services. Practical steps include care coordinators who can navigate housing, welfare, and social needs alongside medical care; shared training programs; and co‑located or virtual hubs where GPs, nurses, social workers and community health workers can coordinate in real time. I’ve seen benefits in local pilots where a social worker or care coordinator joined primary care teams to address social determinants of health, reducing repeated visits and supporting earlier intervention.

- Expand training, recruitment and career pathways
To maintain safe care, you need a pipeline of skilled staff. This means expanding training places, returning‑to‑practice routes, and apprenticeships in nursing, allied health roles and mental health support, plus structured CPD that keeps clinicians up to date with telehealth and new care models. Flexible routes for career progression and strong mentoring help retain staff who might otherwise leave for better work‑life balance or different sectors. I’ve noticed how locally accessible apprenticeships can attract people from diverse backgrounds and reflect community needs more accurately.

- Focus on rural and underserved areas
The workforce plan should include targeted schemes for rural and mobility‑challenged populations—mobile clinics, telehealth hubs, and partnerships with schools, libraries and community centres to host clinics. These approaches keep services accessible without compromising safety and allow staff to work closer to home yet still deliver high standards of care.

- Use data to guide implementation and demonstrate impact
Pilot projects should be evaluated quickly and iteratively. The plan should demand timely data on safety indicators, patient experience and outcomes, so staffing decisions can adapt without delaying benefits to patients.

In short, a workable NHS workforce plan will blend people and processes: safer, stable staffing; care that remains personal and continuous; vigilant safety governance; and strong collaboration across health, social care and community services. When these pieces come together—with joint funding and clear accountability—the system can improve timely access without sacrificing quality. That feels achievable and aligns with what patients like me need: reliable care from familiar clinicians, coordinated across the services that touch our lives outside traditional medical care.
