Childcare and family support must be integral: subsidised or on-site childcare, extended hours for those shift patterns, and school holiday clubs so staff with family responsibilities can work when needed without burning out.

Mental health and wellbeing should be proactive, with confidential, easily accessible support, regular wellbeing checks, and protected time for rest and debrief after difficult shifts. A plan that treats staff wellbeing as essential, not optional, will reduce turnover and sustain safety and quality.

Finally, ensure clear career progression, fair pay, and multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, social prescribers, physios) so staff feel valued and have routes to upskill. These steps will help recruit, retain and support a sustainable NHS workforce while preserving high standards of care!

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care, the plan should prioritise targeted incentives for hard-to-fill areas across Northern Ireland. This means delivering tailored rural, urban deprived and coastal packages with housing and transport support to attract clinicians to those communities. Pair this with targeted competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries to bring more nurses, GPs and allied health professionals into underserved areas and high‑demand roles. Provide clear funded career pathways, protected CPD time, structured mentorship and return‑to‑practice schemes to keep experienced clinicians and newer staff engaged. In my experience, practices in rural NI struggle to fill vacancies; a modest relocation grant and accessible CPD funded time would make a real difference and reduce delays in patient care. Practical examples include bursaries for students from local communities, mentorship networks linking rural and urban teams, and clear routes from trainee to independent practitioner. Above all, ensure workloads are manageable so patient safety remains the priority and high‑quality care is sustainable for communities that rely on these services.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise tailored incentives to recruit, retain and support staff in hard‑to‑fill areas—rural, urban deprived and coastal communities. This means not just pay, but housing and transport support to remove practical barriers to relocation and daily work. Relocation grants, subsidised housing and enhanced travel allowances would make posts in these areas feasible and sustainable, alongside flexible rosters and genuine career progression opportunities so staff see a long‑term future locally.

Beyond money, invest in local pipelines: partnerships with training centres, schools and universities, plus accelerated return‑to‑work routes, mentoring and protected time for upskilling within multidisciplinary teams. In our organisation we’ve seen how continuity of care relies on stable teams; when turnover is high, patients with multimorbidity and complex needs suffer.

Hard‑to‑fill areas also need robust support for safe staffing, supervision, and access to digital tools that enable remote triage and consultations, reducing unnecessary travel while keeping care local. Establish clear rural/urban deprivation/coastal designations with dedicated targets and funding to monitor progress and adapt as needed. This approach supports safer, higher‑quality care while addressing the practical realities staff face in challenging communities.

TO RECRUIT, RETAIN AND SUPPORT NHS STAFF WHILE KEEPING CARE SAFE AND HIGH QUALITY, THE WORKFORCE PLAN MUST PRIORITISE PRACTICAL INCENTIVES, CLEAR CAREER DEVELOPMENT AND STRENGTHENED CROSS-SECTOR LINKS. TARGETED, COMPETITIVE PAY BANDS, RETENTION PAYMENTS FOR HARD-TO-FILL POSTS, RELOCATION PACKAGES AND FUNDED BURSARIES SHOULD BE OFFERED TO ATTRACT PEOPLE TO UNDERSERVED AREAS AND HIGH-DEMAND ROLES, INCLUDING CARE HOMES, DISTRICT NURSING AND MENTAL HEALTH TEAMS. THESE FINANCIAL INCENTIVES MUST BE PAIRED WITH PROTECTED CPD TIME AND FUNDED TRAINING SO STAFF CAN UPSKILL WITHOUT COMPROMISING PATIENT CARE, PLUS FUNDED RETURN-TO-PRACTICE SCHEMES AND ROBUST MENTORING TO SUPPORT BOTH EXPERIENCED CLINICIANS AND THOSE EARLY IN THEIR CAREERS. 

STRONG, JOINT FUNDING AND CLOSER COLLABORATION WITH SOCIAL CARE, MENTAL HEALTH AND COMMUNITY SERVICES ARE ESSENTIAL TO REDISTRIBUTE WORKLOAD AND ENABLE HOLISTIC PATIENT CARE. SHARED ROLES, INTEGRATED TEAMS, AND COMMON DIGITAL RECORDS WOULD CUT DUPLICATION AND UNNECESSARY REFERRALS, WHILE REALISTIC STAFFING MODELS GUIDED BY WORKLOAD METRICS ENSURE SAFE STAFFING LEVELS.

IN MY EXPERIENCE, A RELOCATION PACKAGE HELPED A DISTRICT NURSE MOVE CLOSER TO A RURAL PRACTICE, AND MENTORSHIP SCHEMES HAVE IMPROVED RETENTION FOR NEW GPS. WHEN THE PLAN ALIGNS FAIR PAY, CAREER PROGRESSION AND CROSS-SECTOR COLLABORATION, STAFF STABILITY FOLLOWS, DELIVERING SAFER, MORE RELIABLE CARE FOR PATIENTS ACROSS COMMUNITIES.

From my experience of accessing NHS services in England, any workforce plan must first safeguard patients’ safety and continuity of care even as recruitment picks up. I’d prioritise three things. First, overseas recruitment done responsibly: streamlined visas and credential recognition, but with strong integration support and safeguards to avoid draining health systems in source countries and to protect local training capacity. New arrivals should have a proper induction, language support if needed, and supervised integration so they’re confident in our practices.

Second, safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models: ensure teams have enough doctors, nurses, and allied staff so patients see familiar clinicians, especially for chronic and mental health needs. Safety monitoring and simple dashboards should flag when demand outstrips supply, preventing shortcuts that could compromise quality. In my area, continuity with the same GP has helped my COPD and arthritis neighbour manage care better.

Third, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams: nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied roles must be trained, supervised, and clearly scoped so they can safely redistribute GP workload. This also means strong career development and supervision, so staff stay and quality is maintained. Additionally, offer flexible, non-digital access alongside digital options, with robust data-sharing and patient feedback, to keep care patient‑centred. A plan built on safety, good staffing, and visible governance will improve access without sacrificing quality.

Prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models, cut unnecessary targets and admin burden, streamline referrals with better IT, and secure joint funding with social care, mental health and community services to rebalance workload and protect high-quality care.

From our perspective working with communities across England, the NHS workforce plan must do more than simply fill vacancies. It needs to create a sustainable, diverse and well-supported workforce capable of delivering safe, high-quality care now and into the future. The core priorities should be interconnected: growing domestic supply through training, enhancing retention and wellbeing, and strengthening the data that informs planning and funding decisions.

First, prioritise expanding training pipelines for primary care staff. This means increasing undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and robust university–practice partnerships to grow domestic supply. We should aim for more GP trainees, nursing staff, allied health professionals and healthcare assistants who can build long-term careers within primary and community care. Protected placements are essential so students gain meaningful clinical experience without being bounced around between services. However, expansion must be funded, time-bound and quality-driven: ensure supervision, reasonable caseloads during training, and clear career pathways so people are not lost to the system after qualifying. In practice, this could mean dedicated cohorts in primary care with allocated mentors, integrated teaching clinics attached to local practices, and joint funding streams that cover supervision time and development opportunities.

Second, focus on retention and wellbeing as a core safety issue. Flexible working must be a norm, not an exception: part-time roles, job-share arrangements, phased retirement, and predictable shift patterns help retain experienced staff who know local communities. Support for childcare, family-friendly policies, and proactive mental health services for staff are not extras—they’re essential for reducing burnout and maintaining quality care. In our networks, flexible arrangements have shown real value in retaining skilled practitioners who might otherwise step back, especially in hard-to-staff roles in child, mental health and community services.

Third, develop transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks. Local health leaders need accurate picture of demand, skill mix, vacancy rates, turnover, sickness absence and training pipeline health. By publishing dashboards and conducting independent evaluations, commissioning bodies can adapt plans in real time, stop misallocations, and demonstrate accountability to patients and communities. This data should feed multi-year workforce strategies tied to service design, including co-located and integrated care models that rely on a stable mix of clinicians across primary, community and mental health settings.

Fourth, design the workforce with safer, higher-quality care in mind. That means ensuring safe staffing levels with dynamic rostering, clear supervision, and protected time for professional development. Cross-disciplinary teams and joint training across primary and mental health services help standardise pathways, reduce duplication, and improve patient safety. Practical steps include embedded care coordinators in GP practices, back-office support that frees clinicians from admin, and shared IT systems that maintain continuity of care while protecting patient data.

Fifth, address urban–rural and access gaps. Tailored recruitment incentives for underserved areas, support for remote and hybrid working, and high-quality telemedicine where appropriate can widen access without compromising safety. Localised plans should recognise transport barriers and family realities faced by patients and staff alike, using mobile clinics or community hubs where needed." 

Finally, embed strong leadership and development infrastructure. Invest in frontline and mid-level management, supervision, mentorship, and regular workforce reviews to ensure plans stay grounded in frontline reality. Clear accountability, long-term funding commitments and alignment with the broader aim of parity between mental and physical health funding will help sustain improvements.

In short, the NHS workforce plan should be designed as a coherent system: grow the domestic supply through protected, high-quality training; retain talent through flexible working and wellbeing support; base decisions on transparent local data; and build safer, integrated teams with strong leadership. This approach aligns with our experience that well-supported staff deliver timely, safe and compassionate care, and it helps communities feel confident that the NHS is investing in the people who deliver it every day.

Prioritise tailored incentives for hard-to-fill areas—rural, urban deprived and coastal—plus housing and transport support to recruit and retain staff. Strengthen joint funding with social care and mental health/community services to share workload and sustain safe, high-quality care.

From my perspective, the NHS workforce plan should focus on stability and fairness in funding and career development. A secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlement is essential so trusts can plan recruitment, training, and service expansion without constant policy upheaval. This would underpin sustained workforce initiatives, increase capacity for training, and keep waiting lists down. Clear funded career pathways with protected CPD time, mentoring, and robust return-to-practice routes are crucial to retain both experienced clinicians and new entrants. In practice, that means more funded training posts for GPs, nurses, and therapists, extended supervision for new staff, and funded mentorship schemes to support those returning after a break. For me, when people feel supported and can progress, care quality and morale rise, and we avoid the churn that leads to delays in appointments. Also, flexible working patterns and well-supported remote or home-visit teams help us in older age groups who need timely, local care. In short: stable funding, clear progression, protected CPD, and return-to-practice support are the foundations for safe, high-quality care.

I THINK ANY NHS WORKFORCE PLAN THAT AIMS TO RECRUIT, RETAIN AND SUPPORT STAFF MUST BE BUILT AROUND PEOPLE’S REAL LIVES AS WELL AS PATIENT SAFETY. IN MY EXPERIENCE, CARE TEAMS WORK BEST WHEN STAFF FEEL SUPPORTED, VALUED AND ABLE TO BALANCE WORK WITH FAMILY AND WELLBEING. WITH THAT IN MIND, I’D PRIORITISE THE FOLLOWING:

- FLEXIBLE, DIVERSE WORKING PATTERNS TO RETAIN STAFF AND REDUCE BURNOUT. THIS MEANS MORE PART-TIME AND JOB-SHARE OPPORTUNITIES, PHASED RETIREMENT, AND ACCESSIBLE CHILDCARE SUPPORT OR SUBSIDIES. FOR EXAMPLE, IN A LOCAL PRACTICE, OFFERING FLEXIBLE GP SESSIONS AND SHARED SHIFTS FOR NURSING COLLEAGUES HELPED SOMEONE RETURN AFTER MATERNITY LEAVE WITHOUT TAKING ON A FULL-TIME BURDEN, AND KEPT THEIR EXPERTISE IN THE TEAM. PROVIDING FLEXIBLE HOURS AND PREDICTABLE ROTAS ALSO HELPS STAFF PLAN AROUND CARING RESPONSIBILITIES, WHICH DIRECTLY IMPACTS RETENTION AND MORALE.

- SAFE STAFFING RATIOS AND CONTINUITY-PRESERVING CARE. ACCESS TO TIMELY CARE SHOULD NEVER COME AT THE EXPENSE OF SAFETY. THE PLAN SHOULD SET CLEAR STAFFING THRESHOLDS BY SETTING AND MONITORING SAFE RATIOS AND ROSTERING THAT PRESERVES CONTINUITY WHERE POSSIBLE (NAMED CLINICIANS OR STABLE MDT TEAMS FOR LONG-RUNNING CONDITIONS). REGULAR SAFETY MONITORING AND INCIDENT REVIEW SHOULD BE BAKED IN, SO WE CAN SPOT AND ADDRESS GAPS BEFORE THEY AFFECT PATIENTS.

- TARGETED PAY, INCENTIVES, AND RELOCATION PACKAGES TO ATTRACT STAFF TO UNDERSERVED AREAS AND HIGH-DEMAND ROLES. COMPETITIVE PAY IS ESSENTIAL, BUT SO ARE RETENTION PAYMENTS FOR HARD-TO-FILL POSTS, BURSARIES FOR TRAINING IN PRIORITY AREAS, AND RELOCATION SUPPORT TO RURAL OR DEPRIVATION AREAS. I’VE SEEN HOW A WELL-TIMED RELOCATION PACKAGE AND A FUNDED TRAINING PLACE CAN BRING A SKILLED PHYSIOTHERAPIST INTO A RURAL CLINIC, WHICH DOWNSTREAM REDUCES BACKLOG AND IMPROVES PATIENT OUTCOMES.

- INVESTMENT IN TRAINING, DEVELOPMENT AND PROGRESSION. A WORKFORCE PLAN MUST FUND PROTECTED TIME FOR CONTINUED PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT, ROBUST SUPERVISION, AND CLEAR CAREER LADDERS WITHIN TEAMS. WHEN STAFF SEE A PATH TO GROW—WITHOUT LEAVING THE WORKPLACE THEY KNOW AND TRUST—IT STRENGTHENS LOYALTY AND RAISES CARE QUALITY. CROSS-SKILLING WITHIN MDTS (PHARMACISTS HANDLING MEDICATION REVIEWS, PHYSIOS CONTRIBUTING TO EARLY BACK-PAIN TRIAGE, ETC.) SHOULD BE SUPPORTED WITH GOVERNANCE AND CLEAR SCOPE OF PRACTICE.

- MENTAL HEALTH AND WELLBEING AS A GOVERNANCE PRIORITY. PROACTIVE MENTAL HEALTH SUPPORT, EASY ACCESS TO CONFIDENTIAL COUNSELLING, AND MANAGER TRAINING TO SPOT BURNOUT EARLY ARE NOT SOFT EXTRAS—THEY ARE ESSENTIAL TO KEEPING SKILLED STAFF WHO ARE THE BACKBONE OF SAFE CARE. NORMALISING WELLBEING SERVICES HELPS REDUCE TURNOVER AND SUSTAIN HIGH PERFORMANCE, ESPECIALLY IN DEMANDING ROLES.

- PRACTICAL ENABLEMENT OF SAFE, SUSTAINABLE CHANGE. ANY PLAN SHOULD COUPLE STAFFING WITH ROBUST DIGITAL AND LOGISTICAL SUPPORT—SHARED, INTEROPERABLE RECORDS; TRANSPARENT WORKLOAD DASHBOARDS; AND EVIDENCE-BASED ROLLOUT WITH ONGOING PATIENT AND STAFF FEEDBACK. IT’S NOT ENOUGH TO HIRE MORE PEOPLE IF WE DON’T GIVE TEAMS THE TOOLS TO WORK TOGETHER SMOOTHLY AND SAFELY.

TAKEN TOGETHER, THESE PRIORITIES SUPPORT THE MDT APPROACH I’VE DESCRIBED PREVIOUSLY: MORE PEOPLE IN THE RIGHT ROLES, EMPOWERED TO DELIVER ROUTINE AND PREVENTIVE CARE WHILE CLINICIANS WITH COMPLEX NEEDS GET THE TIME AND SPACE FOR HIGH-RISK DECISIONS. THE OVERARCHING AIM IS TO IMPROVE ACCESS WITHOUT COMPROMISING QUALITY, SO PATIENTS GET TIMELY HELP FROM TEAMS THAT FEEL SUPPORTED AND ABLE TO PROVIDE CONSISTENT, SAFE CARE.

i really think this is a big question and there isn’t a simple answer that fits every town or practice. From my experience in Wales, staffing gaps are real and they ripple through to patients—affecting how quickly people can get GP slots, how quickly community teams can respond, and how safely mental health services are able to operate. I’d rather see a plan that recognises local variation and is funded to adapt, not one-size-fits-all mandates that can’t be delivered in practice.

If I had to name priorities, they would be focused on making recruitment, retention and support practical and locally responsive, while still guaranteeing safe, high-quality care:

- Local, adequately funded recruitment and retention efforts: create flexible, place-based posts that work in rural and coastal areas as well as urban centres. A pool of trained staff who can be shared across several practices or community teams could help, but only with proper backfill so coverage doesn’t collapse when someone is away. In my county, clinics rely on locums and short-term cover, which erodes continuity and increases stress on remaining staff.

- Support for staff wellbeing and realistic workloads: reduce unnecessary admin, protect time for training, and provide good mental health support for staff. If people are burnt out, patient safety suffers and turnover rises. I’ve seen colleagues burn out trying to juggle back-to-back clinics with endless paperwork; it’s simply not sustainable.

- Clear career pathways and training pipelines: more local training places, apprenticeships, and supported routes into leadership or specialisms. GP and nurse training slots are often oversubscribed, and promising clinicians move away or downshift because the next step isn’t nearby or workable. Local schemes that lead to longer-term posts would help.

- Safe staffing levels tied to outcomes: have transparent, attainable targets for nurse-to-patient ratios and equivalent measures across primary, community and mental health services. When staffing is short, patient safety and quality naturally dip, so planning must explicitly guard against that.

- Smarter use of technology to reduce burden: better digital systems that cut duplication, enable effective online triage, and streamline scheduling could free clinicians to see patients rather than chase admin. But tech must be implemented with proper training and ongoing support; otherwise it adds to workload.

- Integrated, place-based workforce planning: better coordination between NHS services, local authorities, social care and third sector providers. Teams should be designed around local needs—district nursing, community therapy, and mental health support workers working together in local hubs to cut travel time and speed up care. In practice, this requires joint funding streams and shared governance so plans aren’t pulled apart by separate organisations.

- Strong ties to education and the local community: partnerships with universities, colleges and schools to attract local talent, plus return-to-work initiatives for those who left the profession. Locally grounded recruitment helps with retention because staff are serving people they know and who understand the community’s specific challenges.

- Transparent funding and accountability: clear budgets, regular reporting on staffing levels, patient outcomes and wait times, and a public commitment to adjust plans if targets aren’t being met. Trust in the system hinges on visible progress, not promises on paper.

I know this is a lot to pull off, and it will require funding, time, and real collaboration between NHS bodies, social care, and communities. My sense is pilots that test different staffing and delivery models could be valuable, provided they’re properly evaluated and scaled only where they work, with the resources to sustain them. Above all, any workforce plan should be judged by whether it cuts waiting times and protects the quality and safety of care, rather than simply increasing headcount on paper.

Ultimately, changes that support local clinicians, value continuity of care, and reduce the burden of admin while linking recruitment to practical, long-term career paths are the ones most likely to translate into faster, safer access for people like me and my family!

Prioritise a joined-up workforce plan with cross-sector recruitment and joint funding for social care, mental health and community services. Shared staffing and workload redistribution will protect safe, high‑quality care and enable truly integrated, holistic patient care.

FROM MY 65+ PERSPECTIVE, THE NHS WORKFORCE PLAN MUST BOTH ATTRACT STAFF TO HARD-TO-FILL POSTS AND KEEP THEM DELIVERING HIGH-QUALITY CARE. PRACTICAL PAY INCENTIVES ARE ESSENTIAL: TARGETED COMPETITIVE PAY, RETENTION PAYMENTS FOR STAYING BEYOND A YEAR, RELOCATION PACKAGES TO MOVE INTO UNDERSERVED AREAS, AND BURSARIES TO TRAIN WHERE SHORTAGES BITE HARDEST. THESE MEASURES WOULD HELP CLINICIANS, DISTRICT NURSES AND MENTAL HEALTH WORKERS MOVE WHERE THEY ARE MOST NEEDED, REDUCING VACANCIES THAT LEAVE PATIENTS WAITING LONGER FOR APPOINTMENTS. 

AT THE SAME TIME, SAFETY AND QUALITY CANNOT BE SACRIFICED FOR QUICKER ACCESS. THE PLAN SHOULD PRIORITISE SAFE STAFFING RATIOS, CONTINUITY-PRESERVING MODELS AND ROBUST SAFETY MONITORING. IN MY EXPERIENCE, STABLE TEAMS MEAN MORE CONSISTENT MEDICATION REVIEWS, CLEARER CARE PLANS AND FEWER ERRORS FOR OLDER PATIENTS. WHERE PRACTICES MAINTAIN PREDICTABLE ROTAS AND ONGOING SUPERVISION, PATIENTS FEEL SAFER AND WAIT TIMES IMPROVE BECAUSE STAFF AREN’T STRETCHED. REGULAR SAFETY AUDITS, REAL-TIME STAFFING DASHBOARDS AND CLEAR ESCALATION PROCESSES MUST ACCOMPANY ANY EXPANSION OF ACCESS, SO WE PROTECT QUALITY AS ACCESS INCREASES. CPD AND RETURN-TO-PRACTICE SUPPORT SHOULD BE EMBEDDED TO HELP STAFF KEEP UP WITH BEST PRACTICE WHILE SERVING COMMUNITIES WITH RISING NEEDS.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise sustainable, funded career pathways across all roles, with protected CPD time and clearly ring-fenced resources for mentorship and return-to-practice schemes. These elements help retain experienced clinicians and support early-career staff who may be tempted to move on if development stalls. In practice, that means guaranteed CPD budgets, formal mentoring relationships, and annual progression reviews linked to competence and service needs.

I also think targeted financial and practical incentives are essential to recruit into high‑demand posts and underserved areas. This includes competitive pay, retention payments for long-serving staff, relocation packages and accessible bursaries to attract students into NHS roles. For hard-to-fill settings—rural, urban deprived and coastal communities—tailored incentives should cover housing, transport subsidies, and flexible working where possible, alongside robust induction and supervision.

From local experience, when staff see a genuine path for development, decent support for moving duties, and tangible housing or transport help, retention improves and care quality stays high. A plan that combines career development with appropriate rewards and place-based supports would address shortages without compromising safety.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high‑quality, the workforce plan must balance flexibility with clear career structure and strong support. Flexible hours, part‑time roles, job‑share arrangements and phased retirement would help retain a more diverse workforce and reduce burnout, particularly for those balancing caregiving or studying. Offering childcare support and predictable rostering would make front‑line roles sustainable and improve recruitment in areas with staffing pressures. In practice, that means I’d like to see GP practices and hospital teams offer more flexible contracts, with protections so staff can move between full‑time and part‑time without penalty, and options for extended shifts or compressed hours that still cover peak times and weekend demand.

Alongside flexibility, a well‑funded, transparent career ladder is essential. Protected continuing professional development, strong mentorship, and dedicated return‑to‑practice schemes would help retain experienced clinicians and support early‑career staff to progress, building confidence and reducing turnover. Expanding training places—undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeships—with protected placements and robust university–practice partnerships will grow the domestic primary care workforce where it’s most needed.

Colleagues I know have left due to burnout or inflexible rosters; addressing that with real flexible working and mental health support will preserve skilled teams and sustain timely, safe care.

AN NHS WORKFORCE PLAN SHOULD PRIORITISE FLEXIBILITY, DEVELOPMENT AND WORKLOAD MANAGEMENT TO RECRUIT, RETAIN AND SAFEGUARD HIGH‑QUALITY CARE. I SUPPORT FLEXIBLE HOURS, PART‑TIME OR JOB‑SHARE POSTS, PHASED RETIREMENT AND CHILDCARE SUPPORT TO ATTRACT AND KEEP A DIVERSE MIX OF CLINICIANS, INCLUDING THOSE BALANCING CARING RESPONSIBILITIES. PROACTIVE MENTAL HEALTH SUPPORT FOR STAFF—ACCESSIBLE SUPERVISION, CONFIDENTIAL COUNSELLING AND PEER NETWORKS—HELPS PREVENT BURNOUT AND SUSTAIN MORALE. FROM CONVERSATIONS WITH COLLEAGUES IN PRACTICE, HIGH ADMIN BURDEN AND IRREGULAR SHIFTS ARE KEY DRIVERS OF BURNOUT THAT UNDERMINE PATIENT CARE AND SAFETY.

WE ALSO NEED CLEAR FUNDED CAREER PATHWAYS: PROTECTED CPD TIME, STRUCTURED MENTORING FOR NEW AND RETURNING STAFF, AND WELL‑RESOURCED RETURN‑TO‑PRACTICE SCHEMES. MULTIDISCIPLINARY TEAMS MUST BE SUPPORTED WITH ROLE CLARITY AND PROGRESSION ROUTES SO EXPERIENCED PROFESSIONALS AREN’T LOST TO OTHER SECTORS. CRUCIALLY, THE PLAN SHOULD AVOID OVERBURDENING STAFF WITH TARGETS, DUPLICATION AND ENDLESS BUREAUCRATIC TASKS. STREAMLINING REFERRALS, SIMPLIFYING PROCESSES AND INVESTING IN USER‑FRIENDLY IT SYSTEMS WILL FREE TIME FOR PATIENT‑FACING CARE AND IMPROVE SAFETY.

OVERALL, A FUNDED, COHERENT PLAN THAT COMBINES FLEXIBLE WORKING, STAFF WELLBEING, PRACTICAL CAREER DEVELOPMENT AND SMARTER ADMIN IS ESSENTIAL TO SUSTAIN HIGH‑QUALITY, TIMELY CARE IN OUR COMMUNITIES AND DELIVER PARITY WITH PHYSICAL HEALTH SERVICES.

i strongly believe from my perspective as an older resident in England, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise stability, continuity and fair, well-supported career paths as the core of safe, high-quality care. I would welcome a plan that recognises the workforce as the backbone of every patient’s experience, and that protects against the churn and short-term policy shifts that so often disrupt continuity of care. In particular, I’d like to see secure, multi-year funding that is ring-fenced for workforce initiatives—not just promises that can be altered with the political tide. This would give training programmes, recruitment, and retention strategies the breathing space they need to work in practice rather than in theory.

Key priorities I think matter most:

- Secure, long-term funding for workforce efforts. A horizon of five to ten years would allow us to grow training capacity, extend return-to-practice schemes, and fund staff well-being and support for longer periods without constant re-justification. Without that security, we end up with short-term pilots that burn staff out and fail to build sustainable teams.

- Expand and stabilise training capacity at scale. Practical steps could include more GP trainee placements in practices, increased nurse and allied health professional (AHP) training places, and funded apprenticeships for support roles. In my area, delays in backfilling roles or replacing trained staff after they move on have created gaps in care at crucial moments. By expanding training and ensuring there is funded, predictable backfill, we protect patient access and reduce the need for patients to repeat their histories.

- Improve retention through better working conditions and workload management. Safe staffing levels, protected time for learning, appropriate admin support, and accessible wellbeing services are essential. When staff feel overburdened or unsupported, the risk of burnout rises, leading to more turnover and gaps for patients who need continuity of care.

- Build clear, long-term career pathways with flexible options. Retention is strengthened when staff can see a path forward—whether through enhanced GP continuity roles, advanced practitioner posts, or specialist pathways in geriatrics and mental health. Return-to-practice schemes should be straightforward to access, with adequate supervision and a realistic restoration of confidence for clinicians who have paused active practice.

- Promote continuity of care through staffing models that support named clinicians and stable teams. My worry is that frequent turnover breaks the thread of trust that is so important for older patients managing multiple conditions. A plan that funds backfill for longer appointments, ensures coverage when a clinician is away, and allows for gradual handovers would help keep care coherent.

- Invest in IT and admin efficiency that actually frees clinicians to care. If electronic records, scheduling, and care planning are well designed and adequately staffed, clinicians spend more time with patients and less time chasing paperwork. This also supports continuity, as care plans can travel with the patient across services.

- Prioritise equitable access across urban and rural areas. Recruitment and retention efforts must address geographical disparities. Remote and community-based roles should be supported with the same career development opportunities as urban posts, including access to training, supervision, and essential safeguarding and geriatric care expertise.

- Ensure safe, well-supported cross-sector workforce planning. Primary care, community services, and mental health teams need a joined-up plan for staffing needs, with shared data and agreed pathways. In practice, that means local accountability for workforce numbers, skill mix, and readiness to backfill urgent gaps without undermining ongoing patient care.

In short, the plan should treat the workforce as a long-term strategic asset, not a variable cost. The evidence of my own experience is that when staff have predictable environments, time for meaningful conversations with patients, and opportunities to learn and grow, patient safety and outcomes improve. Conversely, when funding is unstable or backfill is unreliable, care deteriorates and frustration grows on all sides.

If these guardrails are in place—clear, ring-fenced funding; expanded training; strong retention measures; and systems that genuinely support continuity and safety—the NHS workforce can recruit, retain and develop teams capable of delivering high-quality care, day after day, for the many years to come. I would be willing to see this plan backed with the kind of long-term commitment it deserves, even if it means resisting some short-term policy tinkering in favour of lasting improvements!

A NHS workforce plan should prioritise interoperable, secure IT systems that are simple to use and well integrated into daily clinical workflows. Sharing information across primary care, communities, and hospitals should be seamless to reduce duplication, avoid errors, and help clinicians spend more time with patients, not chasing data. Staff digital training must be ongoing and practical, with cybersecurity embedded in everyday practice so teams feel confident using new tools. Crucially, keep alternatives for digitally excluded patients: maintain reliable phone access, flexible in-person options, and community digital hubs to avoid widening gaps. In our experience, when tech is well supported and doesn’t add unmanageable admin, clinicians can focus on safe, patient-centred care—especially for complex cases that need continuity. The plan should also address workforce sustainability: adequate recruitment pipelines, safe staffing levels and realistic workloads, wellbeing support, and clear routes for upskilling in mental health, geriatrics, and digital care. Funding must cover both technology and the human time to use it effectively; we must protect high-quality, relational care even as we modernise.

absolutely prioritise funded career pathways and protected CPD, plus robust mentorship and return-to-practice schemes to retain clinicians. Expand undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships. Use responsible overseas recruitment with streamlined visas, credential recognition, integration support and safeguards for source health systems!

To recruit, retain and support staff without compromising care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise three things: safe staffing ratios, continuity-preserving care, and active safety monitoring, with strong enabling measures.

Safe staffing ratios: ensure there are enough GPs, nurses and allied professionals to meet demand, especially as hours are extended. Realistic workloads, protected time for complex cases and careful handovers matter. In my area, over-stretched teams have meant anxious patients and rushed decisions. The plan should fund targeted recruitment, retention packages, and postings for rural and coastal areas so patients don’t face longer waits or poorer advice.

Continuity-preserving models: patients fare better when they see the same clinician or a small, stable team. The plan should promote stable rosters or consistent GP access, supported by integrated digital records so continuity isn’t lost during staff changes. This builds trust, reduces unnecessary tests and miscommunication, and is essential for older patients with multiple needs.

Safety monitoring: establish real-time safety dashboards, independent audits and transparent reporting on wait times and outcomes. Use the data to intervene quickly if expansion threatens quality.
