Well-structured MDTs can work, but only if there are formal, funded supervision by GPs or senior clinicians; clear scopes of practice and accountability; and protected time for training and supervision. Invest in training pipelines and clear career progression to make these roles sustainable. Ensure MDTs are integrated with single care teams and robust electronic records so patients have a consistent point of contact. Funding should support a mix of roles and not rely on locums; provide stable contracts and fair pay to reduce turnover. With proper governance, MDTs can ease GP pressure while maintaining safety and continuity!

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise sustainable staffing, safe care and a stable patient experience. It must go beyond simple headcounts and address how and where people work, how they are supported, and how they develop. From our experience, safe care depends on more than vacancies: it needs predictable workloads, strong supervision and teams that can operate across primary, community and mental health settings. 

Key priorities: 
- clear career pathways and protected time for professional development for GPs, nurses, pharmacists and mental-health workers, with formal support for returning-to-practice. 
- strengthened multi-disciplinary teams, with adequate supervision, delegation where appropriate, and shared governance to improve continuity. 
- predictable, market-sensitive pay and long-term contracts to improve retention, plus flexible working patterns (evenings, weekends, part-time and job-sharing) to match staff life cycles. 
- safer workloads and explicit staffing standards to prevent burnout and ensure patient safety. 
- robust recruitment pipelines (regional partnerships, return-to-practice schemes, overseas routes) and streamlined onboarding. 
- enhanced digital and administrative support that frees clinicians for patient contact. 
- deliberate links with social care and voluntary sectors to sustain care at home and reduce avoidable hospital use. 
- investment in estates and IT to create workable environments near clinics. 

This approach aligns staffing with the realities of daily care and transport barriers noted earlier.

Any NHS workforce plan must prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models, with robust safety monitoring to ensure access improvements do not compromise care. It should secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding for training, recruitment and capacity, reducing policy volatility and sustaining quality.

Ensure a secure, multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlement to sustain workforce initiatives and training capacity; invest in interoperable, secure IT and staff digital training; expand undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships to grow domestic primary care staff, safely and sustainably.

i really think a strong NHS workforce plan should prioritise people first—recruiting enough skilled staff and then keeping them well-supported so they can deliver safe, high‑quality care consistently. From my lived experience of navigating GP and community services, the pressure on frontline teams is felt by everyone when rosters are stretched, admin is heavy, and the tech in use isn’t always reliable. A good plan would balance flexible working with robust development and strong digital foundations that together reduce burnout and improve patient flow.

- Flexible, family‑friendly working patterns: The ability to offer flexible hours, part‑time or job‑share roles, phased retirement, and accessible childcare support would help retain a broader workforce. I’ve seen colleagues reduce hours to care for relatives or to manage burnout; when organisations can offer real options for flexibility without compromising care, staff stay longer and bring more experience to the team. Sustained, predictable rotas and the option to balance on‑call duties with protected rest can lower burnout and improve morale.

- Clear pathways for career development and progression: A workforce plan should fund structured career ladders across primary care, district nursing, mental health, and allied health professionals. Regular training slots, supervision, and access to peer support networks would help staff feel valued and stay in roles long enough to develop real expertise. This also includes targeted returns to practice schemes and incentives to recruit and reinstate professionals who have left the workforce.

- Holistic wellbeing and support: Proactive mental health and wellbeing services for staff must be guaranteed. From my own experience, supportive leadership, reasonable workloads, and access to counselling or peer support can be the difference between burnout and sustained service reliability. Investment in wellbeing should be embedded in workforce planning, with leadership training that emphasises psychological safety and constructive feedback.

- Interoperable IT, secure systems and staff digital training (with sensible safeguards): To maintain safety and high quality, we need robust, user‑friendly IT that realises the aims of a joined‑up system. Staff should have access to real‑time patient information across services, with secure data sharing that respects consent. This requires ongoing digital training and protected time for upskilling, testing, and feedback so that teams feel confident using new tools. At the same time, the plan must acknowledge and safeguard alternatives for patients who are digitally excluded—phone‑based triage, in‑person options, and simple, navigable processes remain essential.

- Multidisciplinary, team‑based models: The plan should promote integrated teams—GPs, nurses, allied health professionals, district nurses, mental health staff, and social prescribers working in multidisciplinary hubs. Expanding roles for nurse practitioners and care coordinators can reduce unnecessary referrals, speed up triage, and free up doctors to focus on complex cases. Cross‑training so staff can support adjacent services during peak periods would also help maintain safety and continuity of care.

- Sustainable staffing and recruitment pipelines: Invest in local training pipelines, scholarships, and flexible recruitment routes, including return‑to‑practice programs and international recruitment with structured onboarding and mentoring. This helps ensure steady staffing levels across urban and rural areas and supports the long‑term stability of services.

- Safe staffing and governance: The workforce plan must tie staffing to patient safety metrics—safe nurse–patient ratios, defined escalation processes, and regular clinical governance reviews. Sufficient clinical supervision and a culture that learns from near misses are essential to maintaining high standards even when demand fluctuates.

- Realistic, patient‑centred delivery: The plan should preserve and improve non‑digital access. While digital tools offer real benefits in reducing duplication and speeding access, they must be complemented by human‑facing options and clear handoffs between services to prevent bottlenecks that affect patients and staff alike.

In short, a successful NHS workforce plan is about flexibility, development, wellbeing, robust digital capability, and genuinely multidisciplinary teams working in well‑supported environments. When staff feel valued, have workable hours, and can rely on reliable tech and clear processes, patients experience faster, safer, and more consistent care. This aligns with my experiences of fragmented pathways and long waits—addressing workforce needs is a central lever to unlock better access and higher quality across the system.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care, the NHS workforce plan must prioritise reducing unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks, and streamlining referrals and IT systems to free clinician time for patients. Key steps include simplifying and standardising referral pathways across trusts and consolidating administrative processes; investing in user‑friendly, interoperable IT and electronic records so clinicians can access and update information at the point of care without re‑entering data. This would enable more time for direct patient care, improving safety and service quality. It should be paired with flexible working options, competitive pay, wellbeing support and clear career development to attract and retain staff. International recruitment and return‑to‑practice schemes should be pursued, but only alongside practical changes that reduce workload. Multidisciplinary teams must be expanded—pharmacists, physiotherapists, mental health workers and social prescribers in GP hubs—to spread capacity and ease GP pressure. Real‑time workforce planning and safe staffing norms are essential. In practice, IT and admin relief translate into longer staff retention and faster, more compassionate care. For example, pharmacist‑led minor illness clinics have already reduced GP demand in our area.

I believe any NHS workforce plan must prioritise stable, long-term investment and targeted incentives to recruit and retain staff in the hardest-to-fill areas. For rural, urban deprived and coastal regions, tailored packages—housing support, relocation assistance, and affordable transport—can make posts viable and encourage people to stay long enough to build expertise locally. In addition, secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlements are essential so we can scale training capacity, fund ongoing professional development, and reduce short-term policy volatility that disrupts staffing and service continuity. The plan should expand training pipelines for GPs, nurses, allied health professionals and healthcare assistants, with protected time for education, clear career progression, and strong local mentorship. Practical steps could include two to three year service commitments tied to sign-on benefits in hard-to-fill areas, plus housing and transport supports in coastal towns and rural communities. For urban deprived areas, flexible roles, family-friendly hours and robust wellbeing support would help attract and retain staff who might otherwise leave the sector. Overall, consistency and predictability in funding and policy will underpin safer, higher-quality care across all communities.

Prioritise an NHS workforce plan that backs interoperable, secure IT and ongoing digital training, with robust support for staff and safe, alternative options for digitally excluded patients. Also strengthen joint funding with social care and community mental health to redistribute workload and enable holistic care.

From my perspective as a service user and a working parent, the NHS workforce plan should free clinicians from unnecessary admin so they can focus on patients. Key priorities must include reducing targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks, and streamlining referrals with IT that is easy to use and truly integrated. All too often data has to be re-entered across GP, mental health and hospital teams, and critical information can be missed in the process. If GP, mental health and acute systems shared a single, intuitive platform that auto-populates patient data, flags urgent needs and supports decision-making, clinicians would spend more time with patients and less time chasing paperwork. A connected system would also help NHS111 route people to the right service first time, easing bottlenecks and improving outcomes.

Staffing must be funded for realistic workloads, flexible working, safe staffing norms, and clear progression paths to boost retention. Adequate backfill and robust handovers are essential to prevent gaps when colleagues are off. In short, a lean admin load and smarter IT will protect high-quality care while making roles more sustainable and attractive for skilled staff.

Prioritise clear scope of practice, robust revalidation and appropriate indemnity arrangements; fund protected clinical supervision to support new roles and maintain patient safety while expanding recruitment and retention.

Agree. The plan should clarify scope of practice and revalidation, ensure appropriate indemnity and fund protected clinical supervision to support new roles and patient safety. It must prioritise safe staffing ratios, continuity-preserving models and robust safety monitoring, with tailored incentives for hard-to-fill areas.

Overall, the NHS workforce plan should be transparent, locally driven and adequately funded to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality. It must start with transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding and performance monitoring. Trusts, GP practices and commissioners should share up-to-date vacancy rates, patient demand and workforce mix so shortages can be anticipated and targeted early. 

Particular emphasis should go to hard-to-fill areas—rural, coastal and urban deprived—through tailored incentives, housing and transport support, flexible rosters and stable pipelines that make postings viable long term. We also need clear, funded career pathways with protected CPD time, mentorship and return-to-practice schemes to retain experienced clinicians and nurture new ones. 

In practice, this means visible progression routes from early-career roles into general practice, nursing, pharmacist and allied roles, with adequate supervision and onboarding funding. My own experience shows that when staff have predictable workloads, real development opportunities, and genuine support for wellbeing, burnout decreases and patient safety improves; without such planning, same-day access and outcomes suffer.

Thank you for inviting input on the NHS workforce plan. From our experience of delivering care in England, any plan must prioritise recruiting, retaining and supporting staff while safeguarding the safety and quality of patient care. We’ve seen how staffing levels, team mix and the day-to-day workload directly shape patients’ access and experience, so the plan needs to be practical, locally responsive and sustainable.

- Targeted incentives for hard-to-fill areas: evidence from rural, coastal and urban deprived settings shows that one-size-fits-all recruitment packages don’t work. The plan should offer tailored packages that combine housing support, affordable transport, and flexible working patterns (including part-time routes, weekend/evening slots and streamlining shift handovers). For areas facing housing shortages or long commutes, access to affordable housing near workplaces and reliable transport options can make the difference between someone taking a post or staying away. School places and family-friendly conditions are equally important for staff retention, especially for allied health professionals and nurses considering relocation with families.

- Safe, sustainable staffing levels and workload management: to maintain safety and quality, the plan should link recruitment with robust workforce planning that sets clear safe staffing norms and ensures adequate supervision and backup. This means not only increasing numbers but also ensuring the right mix of skills across primary care, community and mental health services. Administrative burden should be reduced with better support for non-clinical tasks and improved rostering to minimise burnout and enable clinicians to spend time with patients.

- Strengthening training, career progression and local pipelines: expand locally embedded training through partnerships with universities, vocational schemes and primary care networks. Create clear career pathways and mentorship so staff can develop in place, move between roles as needed, and feel there is a realistic future in the NHS. Practical steps include more placements for medical students, nursing associates, therapists and pharmacists, with structured CPD and opportunities to lead multidisciplinary care pathways.

- Multidisciplinary teams and integrated care: the greatest impact on access and quality comes when teams are truly collaborative. The plan should fund and empower pharmacist-led medication reviews, physiotherapist-led musculoskeletal pathways, paramedic or advanced clinical practitioner–led triage, and effective GP workforce support with dedicated practice nurse capacity. This helps distribute workload, maintain safety, and keep patients moving through appropriate channels first time.

- Responsible overseas recruitment with safeguards: overseas recruitment can help plug gaps quickly, but it must be done ethically and sustainably. The plan should streamline visas and credential recognition while providing comprehensive integration support—orientation on local practice, language, and culture, mentorship, and peer networks. Importantly, safeguards should prevent depleting source-country health systems: use return-of-service commitments, cap placements where appropriate, and invest in training capacity in partner countries where possible. In practice, where we have seen a smoother onboarding for overseas staff, with active integration support and clear supervision, retention improves and the quality of care remains high.

- Wellbeing, safety and inclusive culture: staff mental health and wellbeing must be a core element, not an afterthought. Accessible counselling, debrief routines after difficult shifts, and supportive supervision are essential. The plan should promote inclusive recruitment and retention practices, addressing language needs, cultural competency, and flexible arrangements that support diverse staff groups and their families.

- Data, performance and continuous learning: build strong workforce analytics to monitor vacancies, fill rates, turnover, and patient outcomes. Use scenario planning to test how different recruitment strategies perform under demand spikes, and create feedback loops so frontline teams shape ongoing workforce decisions. Tie funding to demonstrated improvements in safety, wait times and equity of access.

In our area, a combination of housing and transport support, plus a careful, ethical approach to overseas recruitment with solid integration, would make a meaningful difference. A well-designed plan that also sustains training, supports multidisciplinary working and reduces administrative burdens will help us recruit, keep and develop staff while maintaining the high-quality care patients expect. We urge policy makers to align the workforce plan with local needs, so that the people delivering care feel supported, valued and able to provide timely, compassionate services to all residents.

From where I stand in England, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise building a strong, domestically trained primary care workforce through clear, well-funded education and training pipelines. My view is practical and rooted in local experience: to keep high-quality, safe care, we must grow the number of people entering and staying in primary care, not rely primarily on short-term recruitment from outside the country. That means massively expanding undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places, with protected placements and genuine university–practice partnerships that are designed around real community needs.

Key priorities I’d like to see are:
- Protected placements and funded supervision: Guarantee placements for students and trainees in GP practices, mental health teams, community nursing and allied health settings, with protected time for supervisors. When supervision is properly funded and expected, staff in small practices aren’t pulled away by admin or non-clinical duties, and trainees get the mentoring they need to develop safely.
- Strong university–practice partnerships: Co-design curricula with frontline teams, ensuring trainees gain real, applicable experience in primary care from first-year placements onward. Local students who train in our community are more likely to return to work here, creating continuity of care and stronger relationships with patients.
- Expand undergraduate and postgraduate intake: Increase medical, nursing, physician associate and allied-health student places, with scholarships or bursaries focused on rural and underserved areas. More importantly, place students early and consistently in primary care settings to demonstrate the value and appeal of local careers and long-term progression.
- Apprenticeships as a genuine route into primary care roles: Develop robust apprenticeship pathways—from healthcare assistants to registered nurses, from pharmacists’ staff to GP practice assistants—that culminate in recognised qualifications and clear, transferable career steps. Such routes can diversify the workforce, improve retention, and help people build in-work experience while they study.
- Local career progression and retention: Build clear career ladders within primary care—nurse practitioners, practice nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, and AHPs—so staff see a future in their local area. Combine this with flexible working patterns, supportive line-management, and access to ongoing professional development, which reduces burnout and turnover.
- Adequate funding for training time and supervision: Practices are under pressure to deliver care while training the next generation. We need ring-fenced funding for training time, locum cover during busy periods, and administrative support to manage placements without compromising patient safety.
- Multidisciplinary teams and integrated care: Train and fund teams that include GPs, nurses, pharmacists, therapists and social care staff who can coordinate around a patient. This not only improves care quality but also helps distribute the workload more evenly, making primary care a more sustainable career choice.
- Focus on safety and wellbeing: Ensure safe staffing ratios and robust mental health and wellbeing support for staff. A plan that values staff health is a plan that protects patient safety; under-resourced, overworked teams cannot maintain high-quality care.
- Rural and community-centred placements: Prioritise placements in rural and mixed settings with appropriate incentives, so learners gain experience in the contexts where shortages are most acute and patients have longstanding relationships with their local doctors and teams.
- Reduce administrative burden through training and technology: Provide training that helps staff use digital tools efficiently, but don’t let tech or bureaucracy erode patient-facing time. Well-designed digital upskilling should free up clinicians to focus on hands-on care and patient contact.

In our local experience, when a GP practice offered a protected student placement with supervisor support and dedicated training time, we saw an uptick in applicants who later chose to train locally and stay. A practical example is a small outreach project that brought in medical students and early-position nurses for regular rotations; over time several participants chose to pursue nursing and general practice careers in the area, which translated into more stable rotas and better continuity for patients.

Overall, the aim should be to grow capacity from within the country, cultivate strong ties between universities and local practices, and create clear, attainable routes into primary care careers. A workforce plan that aligns training capacity with real service needs—while protecting staff wellbeing and patient safety—will deliver safer, higher-quality care and a more resilient NHS.

I’d say the NHS workforce plan should prioritise freeing clinicians from unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks so they can focus on patient-facing care. Practical steps include simplifying referrals, trimming outdated admin processes, and making IT systems more intuitive and interoperable—real-time booking, clear case notes, and less need for re-entering the same data across different systems. In my experience, duplicated data entry and clunky interfaces slow care just when families need timely advice and treatment. 

Second, I’d support expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams—nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied roles—to safely redistribute GP workload. This needs robust training, supervision and governance so patients still receive high-quality care, with clear boundaries about scope and escalation paths.

Third, there must be funded career pathways, protected CPD time, mentorship and return-to-practice schemes. This would help retain experienced clinicians and support new entrants, especially in areas with shortages. Flexible progression and ongoing support have kept people I know engaged and confident in delivering reliable care, which benefits patients who rely on steady access to services.

I believe the NHS workforce plan should prioritise targeted, competitive pay to recruit and retain staff in hard-to-fill roles and underserved areas, plus retention payments for those who stay, and relocation packages to move practitioners to rural Wales. Bursaries and funded training places are essential for high-demand roles such as nurses, physiotherapists, paramedics, GPs and allied health professionals, with clear career pathways to improve retention. To keep patient safety at the fore, the plan must also clarify scope of practice, ensure robust revalidation, and secure indemnity arrangements as new roles are introduced. Funding protected clinical supervision and structured mentorship will help staff grow confidence safely as roles expand (for example, the integration of physician associates or expanded nurse practitioner duties). In my experience of working in a rural area, having supervision and clear permissions made a real difference to the quality of care. Coupled with this, sustainable workforce planning must support longer appointment times for complex cases and reliable staffing to maintain timely access. A comprehensive package like this would attract talent to Wales, keep it here, and deliver safe, high-quality care.

From my point of view in England, a strong NHS workforce plan is essential to keep high-quality care safe while making sure we have enough staff now and in the years ahead. Two strands feel most important: expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams so that GP workload can be redistributed safely, and growing the supply of domestic primary care staff through robust training pipelines. I’ve seen firsthand how stretched general practice can become, and I still believe a well-supported MDT model, combined with consistent investment in training, is what will prevent avoidable delays and protect patient safety.

Priorities I’d want to see in an NHS workforce plan:

- Expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams with clear governance. This means explicitly authorised roles for nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals to manage suitable cases, under strong supervision and with agreed pathways for escalation. Practically, this could include nurse practitioners leading routine chronic disease reviews, pharmacists conducting medicines optimisation and minor-ailment clinics, and physician associates handling certain GP-referred consultations. For safety, every role would operate within a well-defined scope, with mandatory training, formal supervision, regular competency checks and robust prescribing protocols where relevant. A coordinated front door—triage teams that direct patients to the right clinician first time—would reduce wasted slots and free up GPs for the most complex cases.

- Build and fund training pipelines with protected placements. To grow the domestic primary care workforce, the plan should increase undergraduate places, expand postgraduate training, and broaden apprenticeships in primary care roles. Protected placements mean students and trainees spend time embedded in general practice, community nursing, pharmacy-led clinics and urgent care teams, with consistent supervision and clear progression routes. University-practice partnerships should be strengthened, including rural and coastal placements to spread capacity where it’s most needed. This isn’t just about numbers; it’s about quality experiences that equip people to work effectively in multidisciplinary teams from day one.

- Invest in retention, wellbeing and career progression. A workforce plan must recognise burnout risks and support staff with flexible working options, realistic rosters, protected time for training, mentorship schemes and clear career ladders. I’ve heard colleagues describe the toll of long hours and administrative burden; reducing non-cl clinical workload through better IT and dedicated admin support, plus structured CPD, would improve retention and patient safety.

- Ensure safe staffing and data-driven planning. Real-time staffing dashboards, transparent metrics on wait times, and regular safety reviews should feed into the plan. This means knowing not just how many clinicians we have, but how they’re distributed across practices, urgent care sites and community services. Data should inform where to scale MDT roles, where additional supervision is needed, and how to adjust training intake to meet demand without compromising quality.

- Secure long-term, ring-fenced funding with clear evaluation. Short-term pilots can be valuable, but scaling must follow rigorous evaluation and demonstrate sustainable improvements in access, outcomes and patient safety. The funding model should cover MDT remuneration, training costs, IT upgrades, supervision infrastructure and protected time for staff to participate in necessary training and audits.

- Align with patient access goals and equity. A workforce plan that supports MDTs can contribute to more flexible services—home visits, community clinics, and rapid triage—without sacrificing safety. It should also address digital and physical accessibility, so patients with disabilities or limited digital access aren’t left behind.

In my area, I’ve seen how pharmacists leading medication reviews and nurse practitioners taking routine follow-ups can relieve GP pressure and help maintain steady chronic care. If the plan enables properly supervised roles and steady investment in training, we’ll see safer care, shorter waits, and less burnout in primary care. But that only happens if funding is stable, supervision is robust, and there’s a genuine commitment to ongoing evaluation and improvement.

I’m supportive of these changes in principle. They need to be rolled out thoughtfully, with clear governance and measurable outcomes, so communities like mine can benefit now and in the future.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise creating a sustainable, safe staffing model while enabling closer collaboration across health and care sectors. In practice this means three intertwined priorities. First, safe staffing and continuity. Ensure safe ratios for all frontline teams and pursue continuity-preserving working models, so patients see the same clinicians where possible. Use real-time staffing dashboards, safety monitoring and proactive rosters to prevent burnout and maintain quality of care, including in urgent and after-hours work. Second, stronger cross-sector integration with shared funding. Strengthen joint funding and governance with social care and community services to redistribute workload and avoid hospital bottlenecks. Integrated care pathways, joint care coordinators, and timely information-sharing will allow more care to be delivered at home or in community settings, improving holistic outcomes and equity. Third, development, retention and wellbeing. Expand return-to-practice schemes, apprenticeships and CPD; provide robust mentorship and career progression; invest in wellbeing support so staff resilience matches growing demand. In my area, better collaboration between community teams and primary care noticeably reduces duplicated tasks and improves patient experience. Finally, rigorous safety monitoring is essential to ensure access gains don’t compromise quality. Regular audits, incident reporting and transparent workforce data will keep care safe as reforms accelerate.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise place-based incentives for hard-to-fill areas—rural, coastal and urban deprived communities—paired with practical housing and transport support, flexible, predictable contracts and rosters to reduce burnout. It should also invest in local training pipelines, CPD, and clear progression paths to boost retention.

Crucially, we need clarity and protection around new roles: define scope-of-practice boundaries, ensure robust revalidation and indemnity arrangements, and fund protected clinical supervision to safeguard patients as roles expand. Use governance-led pilots to test new models with strong competency checks before widening scope. In our area, combining housing and transport support with strong supervision and clear rules would help reduce vacancies and improve timely access to GP and mental health services, aligning day-to-day needs with a sustainable, long-term plan.

The plan should prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams—nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied roles—with structured training and supervision to safely redistribute GP workload while maintaining safe, high-quality care.

From my perspective living in England, a NHS workforce plan must put people at the centre: we need safe, high‑quality care supported by a workforce that is both skilled and well cared for. First, invest in interoperable IT and secure systems with ongoing digital training for staff, but also safeguard non‑digital options for those who are digitally excluded. In my experience, many older neighbours still prefer a telephone call or face‑to‑face appointment, and insisting on online booking can create barriers. Second, strengthen links with social care, mental health and community services and align funding to redistribute workload. If district nurses and care‑at‑home teams can access the same records and processes as GPs, hospital admissions fall and care remains more continuous. Third, responsible overseas recruitment should be welcomed: streamlined visa routes, clear credential recognition, structured induction and language support, with safeguards to avoid depleting health systems in source countries. Finally, ensure retention through flexible working, improved pay, wellbeing support and ongoing training and return‑to‑practice schemes. Above all, patient safety and safe staffing must be the baseline, with local authorities coordinating to fit local needs. This approach would help older residents rely on timely, high‑quality care.

Strong, well-supported workforce planning is essential if we’re going to deliver safe, high-quality care consistently across Scotland. From my perspective, the plan should balance targeted incentives to attract staff to under-served areas and high-demand roles with solid investments in digital infrastructure and staff development so people can do their jobs well and stay in them long term. A few concrete priorities follow, grounded in what I’ve seen in practice and what concerns families I know have raised about access and continuity of care.

- Targeted recruitment and retention packages for hard-to-fill posts and rural areas. It’s clear we’ll struggle to recruit if roles feel like sinkholes for applicants. Practical measures should include retention payments for hard-to-fill posts, relocation packages that recognise the cost of moving to remote parts of Scotland, and bursaries or fast-track training opportunities for students who commit to serving in high-need communities after qualification. In rural and island areas there is a real tug-of-war between attracting talent and retaining it; explicit incentives tied to service commitments can make a meaningful difference.

- Focused expansion of the mental health and community services workforce. Given the priorities I’ve outlined before—early intervention, rapid triage, and home-based treatment—the plan must prioritise CMHTs, crisis resolution teams, and home-treatment capacity. Staff retention is crucial here: stable teams with clear supervision, reasonable workloads, and access to ongoing professional development will translate into safer, more timely care for people in distress.

- Interoperable IT, secure systems and staff digital training, with safeguards for the digitally excluded. I’ve seen how digital tools can shave days off waiting times and help care navigators serve patients more effectively. The plan should fund secure, interoperable electronic health records, reliable access to IT across settings, and ongoing digital literacy training for staff so they can use the systems confidently. At the same time, we must safeguard non-digital pathways—telephone triage, face-to-face help at local hubs, and outreach for those without reliable broadband or with language barriers. A mixed model that keeps people connected to real help, not just screens, is essential.

- Sustainable working conditions and career pathways. Recruitment is one thing; keeping people in the job is another. The plan should promote flexible working patterns where feasible, protected supervision and supervision time, opportunities for career progression (including nurse associates, physiotherapist and psychology rotations, and multi-disciplinary training), and robust wellbeing and occupational health support to prevent burnout. Clear, visible routes to senior clinical leadership and meaningful professional development help staff feel valued and contribute to improved patient outcomes.

- Commissioning and governance aligned with service demand. Real-time data on staffing levels, patient demand, and wait times should drive deployment and escalation decisions. The workforce plan should include predictable funding pipelines tied to service targets, with accountability for safe staffing ratios, appropriate skill mixes, and outcomes tracking to prevent drift back toward unsafe or under-resourced care.

- Collaboration and pipelines. Strengthen partnerships with universities, colleges, and the third sector to build a steady pipeline—student placements, apprenticeships, return-to-practice schemes, and retraining pathways for career changers. This helps widen access to NHS roles in communities that historically lose talent to other sectors or more lucrative opportunities elsewhere.

In short, I’d like to see a plan that combines serious financial incentives with real investment in people, systems and processes that support high-quality care. It should recognise that staff safety, wellbeing and professional development are not optional extras but fundamental to patient safety and timely access to services. If we get the balance right between competitive pay for hard-to-fill roles, strong IT-enabled care, and robust non-digital access for those who need it, we’ll see fewer avoidable delays, greater continuity of care, and a workforce capable of delivering the compassionate, capable NHS we want for Scotland.

Thank you for considering these points.

From my experience in rural Wales, any NHS workforce plan must guard patient safety as staffing levels fluctuate. Prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity of care—patients do worse when they see different clinicians at each visit, especially with complex needs. Protect staffing through workable rosters, longer contracts in rural areas, and clear escalation for urgent slots so covering gaps never undermines quality. Build in robust safety monitoring: regular audits, shared learning from near misses, and open reporting so problems are spotted early.

Invest in interoperable IT and secure systems with proper staff training, but safeguard alternatives for those who cannot access digital tools. The plan should be a blended model: telehealth hubs for those who can use them, plus reliable phone and face-to-face options. In our area, outreach nurses and mobile clinics work best when staffed consistently and supported by IT that shares records across GP, district nursing and mental health teams.

Reduce unnecessary targets and duplications; streamline referrals; and improve IT usability so clinicians have more time with patients rather than chasing paperwork. A plan that combines safe staffing, continuity and practical tech will help keep access improvements from compromising the quality of care.

it's outrageous that focus on expanding training pipelines—undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeships—with protected placements and university-practice partnerships to grow domestic primary care supply, improving GP access and stability for rural Wales while preserving high-quality, safe care!

From my experience in England, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise building and sustaining a workforce that can work more closely across organisations—social care, mental health and community services—to share the load and deliver holistic, patient‑centred care. For older people like me and for those we care for, the positive impact of integrated teams is clear: less time chasing appointments, fewer handoffs, and more consistent, coordinated support. With that in mind, I would prioritise the following, backed by practical examples from my own community experiences.

- Stronger, jointly funded multidisciplinary teams. Funded posts that sit across GP practices, district nursing, community mental health teams, pharmacy, and social care are essential. From where I sit, any NHS workforce plan must balance the need to recruit and retain staff with the core obligation to keep patients safe and the quality of care high. Third, safety monitoring and governance that keep pace with access improvements. Increased throughput must come with stronger safety checks: incident reporting, regular audit of outcomes, and transparent employee well-being metrics. If staff are overworked, errors rise—so the plan should treat patient safety indicators as a pillar of performance, not a corollary. That requires investment in training, peer review processes, and a culture that learns from near-misses without blame.

Fourth, targeted pay and incentives to attract staff to hard-to-fill posts and underserved areas. Complementing workforce numbers with financial and practical incentives makes good sense. This could include competitive pay for hard-to-fill roles, retention payments for staff who stay in challenging posts, relocation packages, and bursaries linked to service in high-need locations or specialties. Fifth, investment in training pipelines and practical support. A plan that looks only at recruitment won’t last. We need funded training slots in primary and community care, supportive induction and mentorship, and opportunities for mid-career nurses, pharmacists and allied health professionals to upskill toward more autonomous, patient-centered roles. Sixth, flexible, team-based care with a clear local focus. The right staffing plan should enable multidisciplinary teams to function at scale in the community, with enough redundancy to cover absences without compromising safety. Technology can help here, but it must enhance, not replace, human care. For example, digital scheduling and remote check-ins should free clinicians to spend more time in meaningful, in-person reviews with a familiar clinician when needed.

Finally, a local, place-based lens. Rural and disadvantaged urban areas face distinct staffing challenges. The plan should align recruitment efforts with local needs—supporting outreach to train local candidates, forging partnerships with universities, and ensuring services are resilient against workforce churn. I’ve seen how mobile or outreach teams, supported by stable core staff, can keep people out of hospital and closer to the care they rely on at home.

Overall, a successful NHS workforce plan won’t just fill vacancies. It must embed safe staffing, continuity, and safety culture at its heart, funded and supported by meaningful pay incentives and clear career paths. If access improvements are to be lasting, they must ride on a foundation where patients can trust that care is safe, consistent, and of high quality.
